| `setTimeout` and socket callbacks run on libuv's loop, which keeps the process alive while anything is registered | `sleep`, `readable` and `writable` park a task on the executor; the program exits once `main` has returned and no task waits, a synchronous `main` included |
| A `string` passed to a spawned call is a shared reference | It is copied into the task's region; an object, array, `Map` or `Set` is shared, and the task may store only numbers into it (NL2609, NL2615) and keep none of it in memory of its own (NL2610); one holding a `Region`, `Secret`, handle or `nish/threads` value is refused (NL2691), as is any other argument (NL2673) |
| A task that never awaits holds the thread, as here | The same: the executor is cooperative and does not preempt a task |

A program whose output does not depend on how its tasks interleave prints the
same under both.

**Under `--emit-ts`.** An `async` function, `Promise<T>`, `await`, an `async`
`main`, `spawn(f(x))` and `const [a, b] = await awaitAll(f(), g())` are
written as the TypeScript they already are, so the output runs on Node's own
async/await and resumes in Node's order, the left column above
(`tests/emit-ts/async/`). `nish:async` is `nish/runtime/async.mjs`: `awaitAll`
is `Promise.all` over its two to eight calls, and `spawn` starts its task
without awaiting it and keeps it. The launcher of a program that declares an
`async` function awaits `main`, then `settleTasks()`, which waits for every
task `spawn` started, those tasks' own included, before it exits, as the
native driver drains its queue. `await sleep(ms)` is a `setTimeout` that
answers `true`, or `false` at once for a negative `ms`
(`tests/emit-ts/async/sleep`); `readable` and `writable` have no Node
counterpart a task can await, so a program that calls either is
`--emit-ts cannot write readable or writable from nish:async` (NL4017,
`tests/emit-ts/async/refused-readable`), and so is one that calls
`readableWithin`, `writableWithin`, `taskId`, `cancel`, `cancelled` or
`cancelAfter`, since a Node promise is not a task the executor can cancel
(NL4018, `tests/emit-ts/async/refused-cancel`). A program whose spawned tasks print in an
interleaving prints the same lines in another order (`async_spawn`, the
`order` row of `tests/differential/emit-ts-known.txt`).

## Data parallelism: `nish/threads`

`parallelMapInto`, `parallelMap`, `parallelFrom` and `parallelReduce` run a
function over every element of an array, or every index of a new one, on as
many threads as the machine has and the length is worth
([wp29-thread-surface.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp29-thread-surface.md) §4.1). They are imported from
the standard library, and the function is a [function parameter](#function-parameters):
a top-level function by name, or an arrow written at the call — which may read
the `const` locals of the function it is written in
([below](#a-data-parallel-arrow-reads-its-functions-const-locals)).

```typescript
import { parallelFrom, parallelMap, parallelMapInto, parallelReduce } from "nish/threads";

const square = (x: f64): f64 => x * x;

export const main = (): i32 => {
  const src: f64[] = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0];
  const dst: f64[] = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0];
  parallelMapInto(src, dst, square);                         // dst[i] = square(src[i])
  parallelMapInto(dst, dst, (x) => x + 1.0);                 // in place
  const k: f64 = 2.0;
  const scaled = parallelMap(src, (x) => x * k);             // a new array: 2, 4, 6
  const halves = parallelFrom(3, (i) => toF64(i) / k);       // a new array: 0, 0.5, 1
  const total = parallelReduce(dst, (a, b) => a + b, 0.0);   // 17
  return toI32(total + scaled[2] + halves[2]);
};
```

- **The module is ordinary Nish, and its bodies are the meaning.**
  `std/threads.ts` writes each function as the sequential loop, which is what
  runs under Node and what `npm run check` type-checks. The compiler recognises
  the two templates by module and name and lowers one call in each instance —
  the loop over the whole range — onto `nish_parallel_range`
  (`runtime/runtime-parallel.c`), which cuts the range into contiguous pieces,
  up to eight per thread, that the threads claim one at a time as they finish
  the last, and joins them all before it returns. Everything else in the instance is
  emitted as written (`tests/link/par_map`, whose `threads.ll` is the whole
  lowering).
- **`parallelMapInto(src, dst, f)`** writes `f(src[i])` into `dst[i]` for every
  index of `src`. `dst` must be at least as long, which is checked once, before
  any element is written or any thread started: a shorter one panics with
  `parallelMapInto: dst has 2 elements and src has 3` and exits 1
  (`tests/link/par_dst_short`). `src` and `dst` may be the same array
  (`tests/link/par_map`).
- **`parallelMap(src, f)`** answers a new array of `f(src[i])` for every
  index of `src`, and **`parallelFrom(n, f)`** a new array of `n` elements,
  `f(i)` at index `i` — `Array.from({ length: n }, (_, i) => f(i))`. Each
  allocates its result on the calling thread before any element is computed,
  so nothing but the region can hold it while the threads write it, and then
  runs the map: `parallelMap` is `parallelMapInto` into that array, and
  `parallelFrom` the same region over the indices (`tests/link/par_map_new`,
  `tests/link/par_from`). `parallelFrom(0, f)` answers an empty array. The
  rules below hold of their `f` as they hold of `parallelMapInto`'s, except
  the one about `dst`, which nothing else can reach.
- **A short array is the loop it would have been.** A map is divided only
  once every thread's share carries enough work to pay for handing it to
  another thread ([wp20-threads.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp20-threads.md) §8e). How many elements
  that is — the *grain* — is sized per call from a static estimate of what
  `f` costs: 2^21 over the estimate, which counts one per operation, 32 per
  allocation, 4 per call, and a loop's body as many times as its literal
  bound says or 64 times when the bound is not a literal. A map longer than
  the grain is divided into `ceil(length / grain)` chunks, at most eight per
  thread with one thread per core, so the first division is two chunks of
  half the grain: 2^20 units each. That is where a measured body, `(x) => x + 1` at an estimate of 3,
  beat its loop by 1.31x on the minimum and 1.19x on the median, more than
  any difference between the loop and a byte-identical copy of it (at most
  3.3% and 9.1%); at two chunks of 2^19 units the minimum won by 1.16x and
  the median by only 1.04x, within that 9.1%
  ([wp29-thread-surface.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp29-thread-surface.md) §8a). So a body estimated
  at 3, such as `(x) => x + 1` or `(x) => x * x`, is divided past 699,050
  elements (`tests/link/par_map`), `(x * 31 + 7) % 1000` past 262,144
  (`tests/link/par_map_large`), a body with a loop far sooner, and a cheaper
  body later: `(x) => x`, estimated at 1, past 2,097,152. Up to the grain the
  map calls its loop directly on the calling thread, where it inlines; there
  is no hand-off and no indirect call. The estimate counts a call as a call
  and not as the callee's body, so a body that hides its work behind a call
  is divided too little rather than too much. There is no knob for the grain
  ([wp29-thread-surface.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp29-thread-surface.md) §9).
- **The threads are a pool, as many as the cores the process may use.** The
  first region or scope join that divides starts one worker per core but the
  caller's, which is the last of them, and at most 63 workers; they park
  between calls ([wp20-threads.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp20-threads.md) §8e). The core count is
  the smallest of the CPUs online, the process's affinity mask (`taskset`, a
  container's cpuset) and the cgroup v2 `cpu.max` quota rounded up, so a
  program in a container limited to two cores divides two ways, not as many
  as the host has. **`NISH_NUM_THREADS`**, when it is set to a positive
  number, lowers that count and never raises it: `NISH_NUM_THREADS=1` runs
  every region and every scope's tasks on the calling thread, in spawn order,
  and anything that is not a positive number is ignored. It is read once, by
  the first region or join that asks, and it decides only how the work is
  divided: a map's answer and a reduce's bits are the same at any count
  (`tests/run.js` runs every `tests/link/thread_*` and `par_*` program under
  `NISH_NUM_THREADS=1` and `=2` and requires the output it gave without). A
  Node addon (`--emit-napi`) keeps a thread per chunk or task for each call
  instead of a pool, because Node can unload it and a parked worker would
  outlive its code, and on WASI every region and task runs on the one thread
  there is.
- **`parallelReduce(src, f, identity)` is deterministic.** `src` is split into
  `min(64, ceil(n / 2^20))` blocks, each block is folded from `identity`, and
  the block results are combined left to right. `std/threads.ts` does the same
  blocking on one thread, so an `f64` sum is the same bits on one core or
  sixty-four, compiled or under Node — which is not the bits of a plain left
  fold over the array (`tests/link/par_reduce`). The blocks are part of the
  answer, so where block `k` starts, `floor(n * k / blocks)`, is computed
  exactly even where `n * k` passes 2^31 (`tests/link/par_reduce_blocks`, 64
  blocks over 70,000,001 elements). An empty `src` answers
  `identity`. For that to be the fold it looks like, `f` has to be associative
  and `identity` its identity. An arrow whose whole body is one operator on its
  two parameters is held to both: a non-associative one is
  `` `(a, b) => ...` combines with `-`, which is not associative: `parallelReduce` folds each block from the identity and then combines the blocks, which is a left fold only for an associative operator ``
  (`-`, `/`, `%`, `**` and the shifts; `tests/cases/reject_par_reduce_operator`),
  and a recognised one given anything but its identity — `0` for `+`, `|` and
  `^`, `1` for `*`, `true` for `&&`, `false` for `||`, written as a literal — is
  `` `parallelReduce` folds every block from its identity, and the identity of `+` is `0`, not `1`: any other value would be counted once per block ``
  (`tests/cases/reject_par_reduce_identity`). **A named function is opaque**:
  its associativity, and the identity it is given, are its author's promise,
  and a wrong one gives a deterministic answer that is not the fold.
- **Importing `nish/threads` compiles the program with `--threads`**, because
  every worker bumps an arena of its own: `@nish_arena` is declared
  `thread_local` in every module and the runtime is built with
  `-DNISH_THREADS` (`tests/link/par_map`). A program that does not import it is
  compiled exactly as before.

What makes a region safe to run on several threads is checked at the call,
from the whole-program facts, and each rule is reported there:

- **The function writes nothing its caller can see.** A store through a
  parameter, a call that makes one, or a runtime call that writes — `console.log`
  included — is
  `` `bump` writes memory its caller can see at main.ts:10:3, and `parallelMapInto` runs it on several threads at once: a parallel body may read what its caller owns and write nothing but its result ``,
  naming the write, or the callee that makes it (`tests/cases/reject_par_shared_write`,
  `reject_par_shared_write_via`, and `reject_par_console_log`, which names the
  runtime's `nish_print`). A method of an
  [atomic](#atomics-atomici32-and-atomici64) — `add`, `max` and the rest — is
  the one shared write a body may make (`tests/link/par_atomic`). A bounds
  check, an integer division, the length
  check of `new Array(n)` and `panic` are not writes: each prints and exits,
  and nothing runs again to see memory. When several threads panic at once,
  the first claims the program: it prints its whole message and exits 1, and
  every later one waits for that exit without printing, so a failing run
  prints one message, never two or a mix of them
  (`tests/link/par_panic_once`, `thread_panic_once`). Output is a write —
  `console.error` and `process.exit` as much as `console.log`
  (`reject_par_console_error`, `reject_par_process_exit`). Reading a shared
  `Map` or `Set` that an element or a capture reaches, with `get`, `has` or
  `size`, is a read (`tests/link/par_map_table_reads`); `set`, `delete`,
  `clear` and iterating one, whose walk counts itself on the table, are writes
  (`tests/cases/reject_par_map_set`, `_delete`, `_clear`, `_values`). Handing a helper a number, a
  `boolean`, an enum or a `string` — a `string` element of the caller's array
  included, `verify(hashes[k])` — gives it no slot to store into, so it is a
  read (`tests/link/thread_bcrypt_batch`, whose task verifies against the
  parent's hashes). The instance performs every store itself, into slots the
  partitioner has made disjoint, so a function that writes nothing cannot race.
- **A store into an array only this call reaches is not a shared write.** A
  `const` the function binds to its own array literal or `new Array(n)` —
  one whose elements are not stored inline — is *private* while every use of
  it is an element, a store into a slot, `.length`, an array method, a
  `for...of`, or an argument of a function that keeps nothing of it. Such a
  function may fill it, `push` onto it, or hand it to a helper that writes
  through its parameter, and still write nothing its caller can see: the
  helper's writes through that parameter land in the private array
  (`tests/link/thread_task_private`, whose body takes its element apart into a
  scratch array). Returned, stored, pushed, bound to a second name (in any
  declarator), named in an arrow, or handed to a function or a constructor that
  keeps it, the array is shared, and so is every store into it
  (`tests/cases/reject_par_private_kept`; the scoped-task twins below). What a
  private array's slots hold is not private: a store into `rows[0][0]`, or a
  helper that makes one, writes what `rows[0]` reaches
  (`reject_par_private_helper_deep`).
- **Nor is a write into an object's own slots, when the object is one this
  call made.** A `const` bound to the function's own `new` or object literal
  is memory no caller, thread or task can see while the call runs, so a method
  or a function that writes only that object's own fields — scalar state such
  as an `Rng`'s — writes nothing shared: `const r = new Rng(seed);
  r.nextI32()` is a body's own business (`tests/link/std_random`). That is
  the whole of what is admitted. A write below the object's own slots, into a
  field or an element of it, counts as a write into whatever it may hold, and
  once a constructor, a store, a `push`, a `Map` or a `Set` has put the
  caller's memory there, or memory of unknown origin, that write is refused
  as any shared write is: `hs.push(box); hs[0].bump()`, `h.b = box;
  h.b.bump()`, a constructor that keeps `box`, a method that forwards to a
  field's method, `o.a.b = box`, and the same with a captured `Rng`
  (`tests/cases/reject_thread_task_private_object_element`, `_field`,
  `_ctor_alias`, `_capture`, `_map`, `_set`, `_nested`, `_array_own`,
  `_forward`, `_forward_store`, `_array_rng`, and
  `reject_par_private_object_field_rng`, `_array_rng`, `_for_of`, `_held`,
  `_kept`). Freshness is not followed through a call: an object a helper made
  and returned is not one this call made.
- **What the function allocates dies with its element.** A function may build
  strings, arrays and objects on the way to its result. They are given back
  after every element: the function gets an arena scope of its own, so each
  call marks the arena of the thread it runs on and releases it before it
  returns, and a map over a million elements holds one element's temporaries
  at a time (`tests/link/par_alloc`). Under glibc, a program that has divided
  a region or joined a scope on other threads keeps the memory a release
  gives back rather than returning it to the kernel, so an element or a task
  that builds a 1 MB temporary does not fault it in again on every call: 200
  tasks that each build one took 48 ms on 1 thread, against 314 ms when every
  release trimmed the heap. A worker that then finds no work for a second
  gives the memory back to the kernel before it parks, its own heap included:
  after ten rounds of 8 tasks that each build a 16 MB temporary, an idle
  program holds 2.3 MB rather than 68 MB, and after four maps of 1.2 million
  strings on four threads, 2.3 MB rather than 82 MB
  (`tests/link/par_map_idle`). With no worker (one CPU, or `NISH_NUM_THREADS=1`) nothing
  parks, so nothing gives memory back early: what a join freed is kept up to
  the 64 MB at which glibc returns the top of the heap by itself. A region below its grain runs as the loop it would
  have been, on the calling thread, and keeps that loop's costs: 200 elements
  that each build a 1 MB temporary take some 320 ms, as the loop does. It
  compiles with a performance warning,
  NL9012, because every element pays for the allocation and the release:
  `` the body of this `parallelMapInto` allocates per element: `label` answers `i32` but allocates on every call, so each thread marks and releases its arena around every element. Compute the answer without building a string, an array or an object to save both ``.
  Two things make that release unsound, and each is refused. An allocation
  stored into memory, which the escape analysis stops following, is
  `` `width` allocates at main.ts:21:21 and stores the allocation into memory, and `parallelMapInto` releases what a body allocates after every element: a parallel body may allocate only temporaries it drops before it returns, and this analysis stops following a value once it is stored ``
  (`tests/cases/reject_par_alloc_escapes`). And a function that reads or moves
  the arena would see the arena of whichever thread ran the element:
  `` `used` reads or moves the arena, and `parallelMapInto` runs it on several threads that each have an arena of their own: a parallel body may not call `Arena.mark` or `Arena.used`, nor open a `using a = arena()` block, nor call `region`, `regionWith`, `child`, `childWith`, `enter`, `enterWith` or `free` (`nish:region`) ``
  (`tests/cases/reject_par_arena`).
- **A map's result `U` is a number, a `boolean`, an enum, a `string`, or an
  array of numbers, booleans or enums**, because the element's memory is
  released before the next element runs and a worker's arena is freed when
  its thread exits. A string or a scalar array crosses by copy-at-join, and
  the caller then adopts it: as the chunk loop rewinds its arena after each
  element, it moves the answer to the end of the chunk's transfer block, a
  `malloc`'d block of 4 KB doubling to 64 KB, or of the answer's size when
  that is larger (`nish_cross_keep`). Once every chunk has finished, blocks
  holding 64 KB or more in all are linked into the caller's arena's chunk
  list (`nish_cross_adopt`), so the answers stay where they are and the join
  costs one link per block rather than a copy per element; less than that is
  copied into the caller's arena and the blocks freed, so a small map run in
  a loop does not leave a chunk behind on every run
  (`tests/link/par_map_join_small`). Adopted blocks are then the
  caller's arena memory like any other, given back when the caller's scope
  releases what the result was made in, exactly when a copied value would
  have been (`tests/link/thread_adopt_lifetime`); a result the body did not
  allocate — a literal, a string it was handed — is not moved at all
  (`tests/link/par_map_string`: `parallelMap`, `parallelFrom` and
  `parallelMapInto` into a `string[]`, under `churn()`). Anything else — an
  array of strings, of arrays or of objects, a `Map`, a `Set`, a class — is
  `` `name` answers `string[]`, and `parallelMapInto` hands back only a number, a `boolean`, an enum, a `string` or an array of numbers, booleans or enums, which the join copies out of the worker's arena: anything else would point into memory the worker frees or reuses ``
  (NL2348, `tests/cases/reject_par_result_type`; `reject_par_map_result_strings`
  for `parallelMap`), because its copy would have to follow every element.
  `parallelMap` and `parallelFrom` allocate their result before the region, so
  theirs is refused there, before `std/threads.ts` is instantiated
  (`reject_par_map_new_result_class`, `reject_par_from_result_type`).
  A map of 1M short strings, `` `s${x % 100000}` ``, took a median of 23 ms
  on 4 threads and 24 ms on 8, against 38 ms for the same loop written
  sequentially, and peaked at 32 MB against the loop's 55 MB. On 1 thread it
  is the loop's time: 54.9 ms against the loop's 57.6 ms and its copy's
  56.4 ms, minima of 9 interleaved rounds on one machine. It used to take
  72.8 ms there, because the mark sat at the end of the full chunk the result
  had filled, so every element's body allocated a fresh 64 KB chunk and the
  rewind freed it; the rewind now keeps that chunk, emptied
  (`tests/runtime-test.c`'s `test_cross_keep_rewind`). Before adoption, when the
  caller copied every string into its arena one at a time, the map took
  56 ms on 4 threads and peaked at 67 MB; two byte-identical copies of that
  binary differed by 5 ms in the same 7 interleaved rounds. What
  the body allocates for an element is released with that element, also when
  the body stores what it builds into an array literal on the way, which the
  arena scope above does not cover: the chunk loop marks the arena before each
  call and keeps only the answer
  (`nish_cross_keep` moves it to the transfer block and rewinds to the mark;
  on the sequential path, below a map's grain, it copies it out and back).
  A body that builds a 2 KB string, stores it in an array literal and answers
  a 4-byte slice of it, over 1M elements, peaks at 32 MB on 1 thread and on
  8 (63 and 67 MB before adoption), where it used to hold every element's
  temporaries until its chunk ended and peaked at 2.1 GB
  (`tests/link/par_map_release`).
- **A frame that runs a map gives its result back when it returns.** A
  function that calls `parallelMap`, `parallelFrom` or `parallelMapInto` and
  lets nothing the map made outlive it frees the result array, and the blocks
  a string map adopted from its workers, when it returns, as the same loop
  written sequentially does. A result that is returned, stored into a field
  or an outer array, captured by a later task, or nested in an array of arrays
  is kept with whatever holds it (`tests/link/par_map_reclaim_escapes`). A
  function that maps 2^22 elements and answers one of them, called 40 times
  on 4 threads, takes 140.3 ms and peaks at 33.8 MB, where it took 493.3 ms
  and peaked at 658 MB: 1.87x its sequential loop (262.3 ms) instead of 0.56x
  (main against a byte-identical copy of itself: about 2%). One call over
  2^25 elements is unchanged, 251.3 against 252.5 ms, inside that band
  (`tests/link/par_map_reclaim`).
  A string map's result handed to a function whose `string[]` parameter keeps
  none of it, reading it or handing it on only to another such parameter, is
  still freed with the frame: 72 string maps over 2^17 whose frames each pass
  the array to such a callee peak at 20 MB on 1 thread and 22 MB on 8, where
  they peaked at 237 MB. The parameter keeps it, and the frame keeps the
  strings, when the callee stores the array or one of its strings into a
  field, an outer array or a `Map`, returns either, passes it to `new` or to a
  constructor that hands `this` out, stores it through any declarator of a
  statement or through a local alias, or hands it to a callee that keeps it,
  and whenever the callee holds an arrow, such as a map's body; the proof
  covers a parameter typed `string[]` exactly, so one typed `string[][]` keeps
  the strings it reaches (`tests/link/par_map_reclaim_strings`).
- **A reduce's `T` stays a number, a `boolean` or an enum.** It is the
  element, the identity and every partial as well as the answer, folded on
  several threads, so a string would be copied at every combine; a reduce over
  strings or objects is refused at the call:
  `` `(a, b) => ...` answers `string`, and `parallelReduce` hands back only a number, a `boolean` or an enum: a worker's arena is freed when its thread exits, so anything else would point into freed memory; answer a number and fold those, or run it on the thread that called it, `let joined: string = ""; for (const b of words) { const a = joined; joined = a + b }` ``
  (NL2348, `tests/cases/reject_par_reduce_result_type`, and
  `reject_par_reduce_result_class` for a class). Map the strings to numbers
  first — `parallelReduce(parallelMap(names, (s) => s.length), ...)`.
- **`dst` is not reachable from an element of `src`.** A function that only
  reads can still read `dst` through its argument while another thread writes
  it, so an array of `dst`'s element type reachable from `T`, through fields,
  elements and `| null`, is
  `` `(r) => ...` can reach a `f64[]` through `r.cells`, which could be the array `parallelMapInto` is writing: another thread would be writing it while this one reads, so `dst` may not be reachable from an element of `src` ``
  (`tests/cases/reject_par_reaches_dst`). It is judged by type, so such an
  array is refused whether or not it is `dst` at run time. A global `Map` or
  `Set` reaches only what it stores: its own arrays are private to it, so a
  `Map<string, i32>` beside a `dst: i32[]` is not refused
  (`tests/link/par_map_read_into`, `par_map_read_into_keys`,
  `par_map_read_capture`), while a `Map<string, i32[]>` is, through
  `x.index.get(k)` (`tests/cases/reject_par_map_value_dst`). A program's own
  class named `Map` is walked like any class
  (`tests/cases/reject_par_map_user_class`). A reduce writes no
  array of its caller's and has no such rule.

### A data-parallel arrow reads its function's `const` locals

An arrow passed to one of the four forms may read the `const` locals and the
parameters of the function it is written in, and so may an arrow given to a
scope's `spawn`, by the rules of [scoped tasks](#scoped-tasks-using-s--scope).
An arrow given to any other function-typed parameter of a top-level function
captures too, by the sequential rules of
[function parameters](#function-parameters) (`tests/cases/fnarg_capture_local`);
the rules below are the stricter ones a body that runs on other threads keeps.

```typescript
import { parallelMapInto } from "nish/threads";

export const main = (): i32 => {
  const k: i32 = 3;
  const table: i32[] = [10, 20, 30, 40];
  const xs: i32[] = [1, 2, 3, 4];
  const dst: i32[] = [0, 0, 0, 0];
  parallelMapInto(xs, dst, (x) => table[x % 4] * k);   // 60 90 120 30
  return dst[0];
};
```

- **Each name the body reads is a parameter of the body.** The checker
  appends it to the arrow's parameters after the ones it wrote, and the call
  passes the local's value through every instance on the way to the body and
  through the region's context with the other arguments, so a scalar is
  copied and a reference is passed as the pointer it is
  (`tests/link/par_capture`, and `tests/link/par_capture_large`, whose regions
  divide). A narrowing in force at the call holds in the body, because a
  `const` cannot change: `if (w !== null)` around the call lets the body read
  `w.scale`. No closure is made: the arrow is still a function of its own, with
  a direct call to it.
- **A captured reference is read-only.** A store through it — an element, a
  field, `push`, `pop`, `fill` or `set`, through a second name the body binds
  to it, or through an object or an array of the body's own that holds it — is
  a store into memory the caller owns, and is refused as any shared write is
  (`reject_par_capture_element_write`, `_field_write`, `_push`, `_pop`,
  `_fill`, `_set`, `_map_set`, `_alias`, `_alias_object`, `_alias_literal`,
  `_nested_array`, `_param_write`, and
  `_reduce_write` and `_into_write` for the other forms). So is handing it to a
  function or a method that writes it (`_helper`, `_method`). Assigning to the
  name itself is
  `` The arrow assigns to `k`, which belongs to the function it is written in: a data-parallel body reads a captured value and never writes it, because every thread reads the same one; answer the value from the body instead, and read the answers from the array the call gives back, `const kValues = parallelMap([1, 2], (x): i32 => x)` ``
  (`reject_par_capture_assign`, and `reject_par_capture_update` for a `k++`
  after a read). A reducer that assigns to one is shown the same
  `parallelReduce` without the write,
  `` answer the value from the reducer instead, and let `parallelReduce` fold it, `const callsTotal = parallelReduce([1, 2, 3], (a, b): i32 => a + b, 0)` ``.
- **A `let` is not captured**, since it could change between the call and a
  thread's read of it:
  `` The arrow reads `m`, a `let` of the function it is written in: a data-parallel body may read only a `const` or a parameter of that function, whose value no thread can change while the body runs; bind the value to a `const` before the call, `const mNow = m`, and read `mNow` in the arrow ``
  (`reject_par_capture_let`).
- **Only an arrow written directly in a function's body captures.** An arrow
  inside another arrow reads nothing from outside itself, neither the
  function's locals nor the outer arrow's parameters:
  `` The arrow reads `k` from outside the arrow it is written in: only an arrow written directly in a function's body may read that function's `const` locals and parameters, and an arrow inside another arrow reads only its own parameters and the module's top-level names; move the inner call into a top-level function that takes the value as a parameter ``
  (`reject_par_capture_nested_arrow`, `reject_par_capture_nested_param`).
- **`this` is not captured by that name**, nor a field through it; bind it,
  or what the body needs of it, to a `const` first:
  `` The arrow reads `this`: a data-parallel body may read the `const` locals and the parameters of the function it is written in, and `this` is neither; bind it, or what the body needs of it, to a `const` before the call (`const self = this`, `const k = this.k`) ``
  (`reject_par_capture_this`). This is a matter of spelling, not of safety: a
  capture becomes a parameter of the arrow, and a parameter named `this` is
  what makes a function a method to every analysis that reads one. A `const`
  bound to `this` is captured as the object reference it is, read-only like
  any other (`const self = this`, in `tests/link/par_capture`).
- **A captured name is read at the call.** The body runs where the call is,
  so the rules that follow a local of the function through its reads count a
  capture as a read of that local there. Three refuse: a destination of a
  scope's task read through a capture before the scope joins, by any of the
  four forms and on a loop's later pass (`reject_par_capture_scope_dst_index`,
  `_indexof`, `_for_of`, `_large`, `_map`, `_map_into`, `_reduce`, `_loop`), an
  element reference read through a capture after a `push` or a `pop` may have
  moved its storage (`reject_par_capture_stale_record`, `_into`, `_loop`,
  `_pop`, `_for_of`, `_helper`), and an array read through a capture after
  `secret(raw)` took it (`reject_par_capture_secret_moved`), each with the
  rule's own message. Two warn under `--warn-portability`, at the read inside
  the arrow as at a direct one: a record copied into an array and written
  through one copy (NL8003, `tests/link/port_rec_capture_copy`, and
  `port_rec_capture_quiet` for a read before the write), and a byte offset
  compared with a count or answered by the arrow, which stores it in the
  form's array (NL8001, `tests/link/port_str_capture_offset`,
  `port_str_capture_result`). A captured name is not a parameter of the
  arrow to NL8009, which reports it where its function declares it
  (`tests/link/port_num_capture_wide`).
- **Some values are never captured**: a `Mutex`, its guard, a `Channel` or a
  scope, which are shared only by their own block's rules, a `Result`, a value
  that may be absent, a `Secret`, or anything that reaches one of them:
  `` The arrow reads `m`, which is `Mutex<i32>`, and a data-parallel body cannot capture it: a scope, a lock, a guard or a channel is shared only by the rules of its own block ``
  (`reject_par_capture_mutex`, `_guard`, `_channel`, `_scope`, `_result`,
  `_maybe`, `_secret`; `_mutex_field` for a lock in a field of a captured
  object, `_mutex_map` for one in a `Map`'s values). A body that runs a data-parallel form of its own is
  refused as a shared write, captures or not (`reject_par_capture_nested_parallel`).
- **`dst` is not reachable from a capture either.** A captured array of `dst`'s
  element type, or a captured value that reaches one, could be `dst`, which
  other threads are writing while the body reads it:
  `` `(x) => ...` reads `dst`, and can reach a `i32[]` through `dst`, which could be the array `parallelMapInto` is writing: another thread would be writing it while this one reads; a captured array is known not to be `dst` only when one of the two is a `const` bound to an array of its own, such as a literal or a `new Array`, and the other is another such `const` or a parameter ``
  (`reject_par_capture_dst`, `_dst_alias`, `_dst_field`, `_dst_param`;
  `_self_field_dst` for `self.out` while `this.out` is `dst`, and
  `_generic_same_dst`, refused in each of two instantiations). A
  capture is a binding the call can name, so one case is admitted by
  identity: a captured array and a `dst` that are two different bindings, one
  of them a `const` bound to an array of its own and the other another such
  `const` or a parameter of the function, as `table` and `dst` are above. A
  fresh array is memory no binding held before it was made, and a parameter's
  value was fixed before the function ran (`tests/link/par_capture`, where a
  parameter table, and two fresh `const`s in a generic function, are
  admitted). Two parameters may be one array and are refused. `parallelMap`
  and `parallelFrom` allocate their own `dst`, which no capture can reach.
- **A fresh `dst` nothing was handed is apart from every capture** (#612).
  When `dst` is a `const` bound to an array of its own, and nothing before the
  call — or in a loop around the call that does not also declare it, or in a
  function written inside — names it except to index it or read a member, then
  no capture can reach it: the only way into a value is through a binding, and
  none was given this one. So the body may read a `parallelMap` result, a
  config object or a `const self = this` beside it
  (`tests/link/par_into_fresh_pipeline`, `par_into_fresh_object`); indexing
  it, reading `d.length`, calling `d.fill(0)` or walking it with `for...of`
  first hands it to no one (`par_into_fresh_reads`). Anything that hands
  `dst` on first is refused with the message above: a store `p.arr = d` or
  `this.tab = d` (`reject_par_into_store_field`, `_this_field`), an argument
  `keep(h, d)` or `ts.push(d)` (`_helper`, `_push`), an alias `const e = d`
  (`_alias`), a branch `c ? d : w` (`_ternary`), a holder `new Holder(d)`
  (`_holder`), a store after the call inside a loop around it
  (`_loop_store`, and `_loop_store_while`, `_do`, `_for_of` for the other
  loops) — the outermost such loop, so a store after an inner loop
  inside an outer one counts (`_nested_loop`) — a hand-on on one branch of
  an `if` (`_if_branch`), an
  earlier call writing the same `dst` (`_twice`), `dst` passed as the call's
  own `src` (`_as_src`), and the arrow reading `dst` itself (`_captured`). A
  `dst` bound to a captured array is no fresh `const` (`_from_capture`). The
  rule asks for the one binding of that name in its function, so a `dst`
  whose name is declared twice there keeps the stricter rule above
  (`_shadow`).

<a id="scoped-tasks-using-s--scope" style="scroll-margin-top: 65px"></a>

## Scoped tasks: `using s = scope()`

A scope runs a handful of different functions at once, each on a thread of its
own, and joins them all when the block that declares it ends
([wp29-thread-surface.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp29-thread-surface.md) §4.2). It is the shape
`parallelMapInto` cannot take: work that is not one function over one array.

```typescript
import { scope } from "nish/threads";

const sumOf = (xs: f64[]): f64 => { /* ... */ return 7.0; };
const primesBelow = (n: i32): i32 => { /* ... */ return 168; };

export const main = (): i32 => {
  const xs: f64[] = [1.5, 2.5, 3.0];
  const sums: f64[] = [0.0];
  const counts: i32[] = [0];
  {
    using s = scope();
    s.spawn(sumOf, xs, sums, 0);           // sums[0] = sumOf(xs)
    s.spawn(primesBelow, 1000, counts, 0); // counts[0] = primesBelow(1000)
  }                                        // both have run, and both answers are stored
  console.log(`${sums[0]} ${counts[0]}`);  // 7 168
  return 0;
};
```

- **`s.spawn(entry, arg, dst, at)`** runs `entry(arg)` on a thread of its own
  and stores the answer in `dst[at]` (`tests/link/thread_scope_basic`). `entry`
  is a [function parameter](#function-parameters): a top-level function named
  at the call, or an arrow written there, which may read its function's
  `const` locals (below). `at` is checked at the spawn and
  again when the answer is stored; out of range is
  `spawn: destination index 3 is out of range for an array of 1 elements` and exit 1.
- **`s.spawn(entry, arg)` and `s.spawn(() => ...)` have no destination.** The
  task runs as any other does and its scope stores nothing when it joins, so
  `entry` answers `void`: it is seen through the guard of a
  [`Mutex`](#a-lock-that-owns-its-data-mutext) its argument or a capture
  reaches, or through a [`Channel`](#channels-channelt) it sends on
  (`tests/link/thread_task_void`, `thread_task_arrow`). A block body is `void`
  without an annotation. An entry that answers a value is
  `` `sumOf` answers `i32`, and a `spawn` without a destination stores nothing: a task's answer is kept only by `s.spawn(entry, arg, dst, at)`, which stores it in `dst[at]` when the scope joins, so make the task answer `void` or give it a destination, `const answer2 = new Array<i32>(1)` above the scope's block and `s.spawn(sumOf, xs, answer2, 0)` ``
  (NL2511, `tests/cases/reject_thread_task_void_result`, and `_arrow` for
  `() => sumOf(xs)`). TypeScript would spell the three forms as overloads;
  the checker picks `ThreadScope`'s method by the number of arguments,
  `spawnWith` for two and `spawnThunk` for one, and under Node every form
  reaches `spawn`, which runs a task without a slot at once
  ([RUN_UNDER_NODE.md](../../RUN_UNDER_NODE.md)).
- **An arrow task reads its function's `const` locals and parameters**, which
  is the whole spelling of a task that needs more than one value:

  ```typescript
  {
    using s = scope();
    s.spawn(() => binInto(xs0, hist));   // xs0: a `const` array; hist: a `Mutex`
    s.spawn(() => binInto(xs1, hist));
  }
  ```

  Each name the arrow reads is appended to its parameters, as a
  [data-parallel arrow](#a-data-parallel-arrow-reads-its-functions-const-locals)'s
  is, and copied into the task's payload at the spawn beside its argument; the
  task reads it on its own thread when the scope joins. A capture **is the
  task's argument to every rule of this section**: the parent may not write
  what it reaches before the join, however it does so — a store, a second name
  for it, a helper, a `new` whose constructor writes it or keeps `this` in it,
  in a scope bound by any declarator of its `using`
  (`tests/cases/reject_thread_task_capture_parent_write`, `_alias`, `_helper`,
  `_new`, `_this_escape`, `_declarator`); a destination is never captured
  (`_dst`); the task writes nothing its caller can see except through a guard,
  a constructor it runs included (`_task_write`, `_task_new`,
  `_task_this_escape`); a `Mutex` it captures is one the parent may not lock
  before the join (R7, `_mutex_lock`) and that it may reach only as a capture
  or a field of one (R8,
  `` The task's arrow reads `o`, which is `Outer` and reaches a `Mutex` through `o.inner.m`: a captured value is the task's argument, … ``,
  NL2510, `_mutex_deep`); the parent's `orReturn` before the join is refused
  (NL2394, `_or_return`); a captured element reference is read at the join,
  so a `push` that may move its storage before the end of the block is
  NL2290 (`_stale_record`, `_stale_join`, and
  `reject_thread_task_arg_stale_join` for a task's argument, read at the join
  the same way); and an array moved into a `Secret` is not read again
  (NL2445, `_secret_moved`). A `let` is not captured, since it could change
  before the task runs (NL2506, `_let`), nor `this` (NL2507, `_this`; a `const
  self = this` is captured as the reference it is,
  `tests/link/thread_task_arrow`), and a captured name is never assigned
  (NL2508, `_assign`). A guard, a channel, a scope, a `Result`, a value that
  may be absent and a `Secret` are never captured:
  `` The arrow reads `ch`, which is `Channel<i32>`, and a task cannot capture it: a guard, a channel or a scope is shared only by the rules of its own block; a task reaches a channel through its argument, `s.spawn(entry, arg)`, where the scope counts its senders ``
  (NL2509, `_guard`, `_channel`, `_secret`). An arrow inside a task's arrow
  reads only its own parameters and the module's top-level names (NL2501, `_nested`). The arrow is lifted into a function
  named after the one it is written in and a counter (`main$arrow0`), which
  is the name a debugger or a profiler shows for the task's thread.
- **A task runs when its scope joins, not when it is spawned.** Joining a
  scope runs every task it was given at once — the first on the thread that
  opened the scope and each other on a thread of its own, so `N` tasks start
  `N - 1` threads — waits for all of them, and then stores each answer in the
  order the tasks were spawned, on the thread that opened the scope. That is
  what makes a scope free of races: while the tasks run, the thread that opened the scope is
  waiting for them, the tasks write nothing another can see (below), and every
  store into the program's memory is made after the last task has finished. So
  a task may be handed any argument — an array, an object.
- **`scopeWithStack(bytes)` is a scope whose tasks have a stack of at least
  `bytes` bytes**, for a task that recurses deeper than a thread's default
  stack allows (8 MiB on Linux): `using s = scopeWithStack(64 * 1024 * 1024)`
  (`tests/link/thread_stack_deep`, a million calls deep on 256 MiB; under an
  8 MiB `ulimit -s` the same program faults with `scope()`, and with
  `scopeWithStack(131072)` on its guard page, `tests/link/thread_stack_fixtures`).
  It covers a scope's tasks only: `parallelMap`, `parallelFrom` and the other
  data-parallel calls run on the pool's workers, whose stack is the platform's
  default. It is a scope in every other rule. Its tasks all run on new
  threads, a thread each, none on the thread that opened it; each thread's
  stack is `bytes` rounded up to the page, with a guard page below it, so a task that still overflows faults rather than
  writing past it. If one cannot be started the program ends with exit 1 and
  `nish: cannot start a thread for scopeWithStack: out of threads or of memory for its stack`
  when the system is out of either, or
  `nish: cannot start a thread with the stack scopeWithStack asked for` when
  it refuses the size. The
  smallest size is 131072 (128 KiB, the largest `PTHREAD_STACK_MIN` among the
  targets): a number written at the call below it is refused,
  `` `scopeWithStack(4096)` asks for a stack below the minimum of 131072 bytes: no target can start a thread on less, and a task that ran on it would overflow before it did any work; ask for at least 131072, `scopeWithStack(131072)` ``
  (NL2584, `tests/cases/reject_thread_stack_small`, `_negative`), and a
  computed one panics when the scope is made,
  `scopeWithStack: a stack of 65536 bytes is below the minimum of 131072`
  and exit 1 (`tests/link/thread_stack_computed_small`). Under Node, on WASI
  and wasm32 (no threads: every task runs on the one thread, in spawn order)
  and in a build without `--threads`, the size is checked the same way and has
  no other effect, so a program that needs the stack needs it from Node too
  (`node --stack-size`).
- **A destination is a fresh `const` array that is never handed on, and until
  the block ends the scope's thread neither reads a destination nor writes
  what a task may read.** Natively a task runs, and its answer is stored, when
  the scope joins; under Node each runs and stores where it is spawned. Two
  rules keep the program's meaning the same either way:
  - A `spawn`'s destination is a `const` local bound to a literal array or
    `new Array(...)` in the same function, used only by index, `.length`, its
    methods, a `for...of` and as a destination — never an argument, a task's
    argument, a stored value or a returned one — so nothing else can reach it.
    Anything else is
    `` The destination of this `spawn` must be a `const` local bound to a fresh array (a literal or `new Array`), used only by index, `.length`, its methods and as a destination: a scope's tasks run, and store their answers, when its block ends, and under Node each runs and stores where it is spawned, so a destination is a fresh `const` array that is never handed on, and between a scope's first `spawn` and the end of its block its thread neither reads a destination nor writes memory a task may read ``
    (`tests/cases/reject_thread_region_dst_not_fresh`, and
    `reject_thread_region_dst_as_arg` for one handed to a later task).
  - From the first statement of the block that holds a `spawn` on the scope
    to the block's end — a `return`'s value aside, computed after the join —
    the program may not read a destination a task of the scope has been given
    by then (`` This reads `sums`, a destination of a task of `s`, before the scope joins: … ``,
    `tests/cases/reject_thread_region_read`), and may not write memory a task
    could read. A task reads only what its argument reaches, so a store is
    fine into the own slots of a `const` bound to a fresh array or object
    literal that is never handed on, and a call is fine unless it writes
    through a pointer it is handed; a function that only fills an array it
    allocates, such as one that builds and returns a row, writes nothing a task
    can see. Every other write is refused, whatever alias it goes through —
    a store, `push` or `pop`, `Arena`, a call that writes through its
    argument, a task of another scope, whose join stores
    (`reject_thread_region_write`, `reject_thread_region_alias_write`,
    `reject_thread_region_call_write`). A constructor is a call: a `new`
    whose constructor writes through an argument, directly or through a
    constructor it calls, is
    `` `new Bump` writes memory a task of `s` may read, before the scope joins: … ``
    (`tests/cases/reject_thread_region_new_write`, and `_declarator` for the
    second declarator of a statement, `_nested` for a constructor that calls
    one, `_this` for one that hands `this` to its argument, which is a store
    through that argument). A write counts however deep it lands in what the
    argument reaches: a field of a field, a field of an element, through a
    `const` that names one, a `for...of` variable over one, a helper, or a
    method of what a field holds (`reject_thread_region_new_deep`,
    `_new_element`, `_new_helper`, `_new_method`, `_call_deep`,
    `_call_element`, `_call_alias`, `_call_loop`). Its stores into
    the fresh object itself are not counted, so `new Point(3, 4)` is fine
    there (`tests/link/thread_task_private`). An object a function or a
    constructor made itself is its own memory, and a write into it counts
    against nothing, until memory an argument reaches may have got into it:
    stored into a field or an element at any depth, pushed, put there by a
    method or a function it was handed to, kept by its constructor from an
    argument, or any non-number value rooted at it — the object, a field or
    an element of it at any depth, a constructor's `this` or `this.f` — used
    as a value anywhere but a read, a comparison or an argument the checker
    follows into its callee: the right side of an assignment, a `const`'s
    initialiser, an element of an array literal, a property of an object
    literal, `{ k: v }` or `{ k }`, an argument of `push`, of a `Map` or `Set`
    method or of a call, an arm of a `?:`. Each position is refused for each
    form of the value, a local, a field, an element and `this.f`
    (`reject_thread_region_escape_<position>_<form>`, with positions
    `assign`, `alias`, `array`, `object`, `shorthand`, `push`, `call`,
    `ternary` and `element`, forms `local`, `member`, `index` and
    `this_field`, and `_this` for the bare `this` in every position but
    `shorthand`, which cannot name it). A `Map` or a `Set` keeps exactly what
    its methods are handed — `set`'s key and value, `add`'s element,
    `getOrInsert`'s from `nish/map` — so each is a store into the table, as a
    `push` is (`reject_thread_region_map_value_param`, `_map_fused_value_param`,
    `_map_own_subpath`, `_map_route_subpath`, `_map_route_value_param`,
    `_set_own_subpath`), and its methods write only the table's own storage,
    never what it holds. What a container gives back is its element: what
    `get` or `getOrInsert` answers, and the `const` variable of a `for...of`
    over an array, a `Set`, or a `Map`'s `keys()` or `values()`, is memory
    below that container, so a write through it counts against what was
    stored into the container, and a store through it is a store into the
    container (`_readback_get`, `_readback_get_or_insert`,
    `_readback_nested`, `_readback_store_alias`, `_table_param_store`,
    `_walk_array_param`, `_walk_array_twice`, `_walk_values`, `_walk_keys`,
    `_walk_set_param`, `_walk_array_store`, `_walk_set_store`). So a call
    that answers a table or what one holds — `getOrInsert(m, …)`, `m.set(…)`,
    `s.add(…)` — is a value rooted at that table, and escapes it wherever a
    name would (`reject_thread_region_call_escape_<position>_<form>`, with
    positions `push`, `field`, `index`, `array` and `object`, forms `goi`,
    `set_chain` and `add_chain`, and `_ternary_goi`, `_nullish_get`,
    `_let_init_goi`, `_let_assign_goi`, `_table_arg_set_chain`). Only a call
    that keeps what it is handed stores it — `set` its key and value, `add`
    its element, `getOrInsert` its key and default — so a lookup, `has`,
    `get` or `delete`, keeps nothing (`reject_thread_region_table_key_set`,
    `_table_key_get_or_insert`); and a number, a string or a `boolean` read
    back through `| undefined`, as `m.get(k) ?? 0`, names no memory. A
    lookup in an argument's table, `has` or `get`, reads it and writes
    nothing (`tests/link/thread_scope_region_param_lookup`). A `?:`
    or a `??` stored somewhere may be either of its sides. Two values may
    be anything where they are written through: an `x ?? y`, and the
    variable of a walk of anything else —
    a `Channel`'s messages are another task's. An object literal
    whose property is an argument's memory carries it however it is written
    (`reject_thread_region_literal_object_param`, `_shorthand_param`,
    `_array_object_param`, `_field_object_param`, `_push_object_param`,
    `_new_object_param`, `_object_const_param`, `_object_method_param`). A
    write below such a slot counts against the arguments
    whose memory may be there, or against all of them when that cannot be
    told (`reject_thread_region_new_alias_field`, `_alias_push`,
    `_alias_element`, `_alias_const`, `_alias_helper`, `_alias_method`,
    `_alias_item`, `_call_wrap`, `_fresh_field`, `_fresh_method_bind`,
    `_fresh_attach`, `_fresh_push`, `_fresh_element`, `_fresh_array_field`,
    `_fresh_nested`, `_fresh_bump_method`, `_fresh_const`, `_fresh_ctor_field`,
    `_fresh_literal`, `_fresh_escape`, `_fresh_held`, `_fresh_held_temp`,
    `_fresh_captured`, `_this_local`, `_this_ternary`,
    `_this_literal`, `_this_object`). A constructor that keeps what it is
    handed keeps it per argument, so one that keeps the caller's own array, or
    pushes an argument's object onto an array it made, writes nothing of the
    task's (`tests/link/thread_scope_region_fresh_object`,
    `thread_scope_region_kept_own`), and a call that only writes its argument,
    or returns an object of its own, keeps nothing of the caller's in it:
    `w = build(h)` on a function that returns a fresh object, and
    `c.reset(h.nums[0])` on a fresh counter followed by writes into `c`
    (`thread_scope_region_own_handoff`). So a `Map` or a `Set` a function
    makes and fills itself writes nothing of the task's
    (`thread_scope_region_map_set`, `thread_scope_region_map_get_or_insert`,
    `thread_scope_region_set_add`), and so does one that walks, memoises
    or indexes a table of its own, or writes through what it reads back out
    of a container of fresh objects it made
    (`thread_scope_region_own_tables`, `thread_scope_region_read_back`). A
    map handed to `set` as a named `const` escapes, as any own object handed
    to a table does, so a write into it counts against every argument: build
    a nested table from what `get` reads back instead. A task argument read out of a
    variable — `s.spawn(f, ps[0], out, 0)`, or either arm of a `?:` or `??` —
    hands that variable on, so a store into its elements or fields before the
    join is refused too: a record element is the address of its slot, and the
    task reads it at the join (`tests/cases/cg_sec_scope_record_arg`). And
    `r.orReturn()` on a `Result` is refused in the same stretch, between the
    first `spawn` and the end of the block, because its early return would
    leave the scope unjoined (NL2394, `tests/cases/cg_sec_scope_or_return`).

  The rules are local because memory is reached only through parameters and
  what a function allocates: a module constant is a number, a `boolean` or a
  string, and nothing is `static`. N tasks over N arrays of the destination's
  own type, built before the scope, in the spawning loop or after the first
  spawn, all compile (`tests/link/thread_scope_many_arrays`).
- **The join is emitted at every exit of the block**: its end, a `return` —
  before the returned value is computed, so the value can read what the tasks
  stored — and a `break` or `continue` that leaves the block
  (`tests/link/thread_scope_exit_paths`). It sits inside every arena scope
  around it, which releases only after the join, and an argument a task is
  handed is never given back by a loop's pass before the join reads it
  (`tests/link/thread_scope_nested_arena`, which also nests one scope inside
  another). Since the join comes first, spawning gives up no memory: a
  function, a loop's pass or a `using a = arena()` block that hands a task an
  array it made still gives that array back when it ends, after the join,
  unless the task keeps it — answers it, or stores it where it outlives the
  task — or the frame keeps it past its end by any other route
  (`tests/link/thread_scope_reclaim`, whose peak resident memory
  `tests/run.js` bounds at every thread count, and
  `thread_scope_reclaim_escapes`, which reads each route after the memory is
  reused). A panic ends the process and joins nothing (`throw` is refused by
  Phase 0, `reject_throw`).
- **A scope is introduced by `using`, and `using` takes only a scope, a
  [`Mutex`'s lock](#a-lock-that-owns-its-data-mutext) or an
  [`arena()`](builtins.md#using-a--arena).** A scope bound any other way is
  `` `scope()` must be the initialiser of a `using` declaration: a scope joins its tasks when the block that declares it ends, so a scope bound any other way would be one nobody joins; declare it as `using s = scope()` ``
  (`tests/cases/reject_thread_scope_not_using`), and a `using` of anything else is
  `` `using` takes only `scope()` or a `Mutex`'s `lock()` from `nish/threads`, or the builtin `arena()`, in this version: they are the values whose disposal the language defines — a scope joins its tasks, a guard releases its lock, an arena releases what its block allocated — so a `using` of anything else would promise a disposal nothing performs ``
  (`tests/cases/reject_thread_using_not_scope`). A `using` declaration is a
  statement of a block; as the body of an `if` or a loop it is
  `` A `using` declaration must be a statement of a block, `{ ... }`: its scope joins when that block ends, and a single-statement body is not a block ``
  (`tests/cases/reject_thread_using_placement`), and in a `case` clause it is
  refused as every declaration there is. Outside a declaration `using` is an
  ordinary identifier, as in TypeScript (`tests/parser/using.ts`).
- **A scope never leaves its block.** It is only ever the receiver of a `spawn`
  statement; passed, stored, returned or copied it is
  `` A `ThreadScope` can only be the receiver of a `spawn` statement: passed, stored, returned or copied, it could be given a task after its block has joined it ``
  (`tests/cases/reject_thread_scope_escapes`). That, and the join at every exit,
  is the whole proof that every task is joined: there is no handle to forget.
- **`[Symbol.dispose]` is `nish/threads`'s alone.** `ThreadScope` and
  `MutexGuard` declare one, so TypeScript and Node accept `using s = scope()`
  and `using g = m.lock()`; the compiler emits the join and the release itself
  and never calls it. `Channel`'s `[Symbol.iterator]`, Node's way into a
  `for...of`, is the one other computed name, and is `nish/threads`'s alone
  too: anywhere else it is refused as every computed name is (NL1041). Any other class's is
  `` `Handle` cannot declare `[Symbol.dispose]`: in this version `using` takes only `scope()` or a `Mutex`'s `lock()` from `nish/threads`, or the builtin `arena()`, whose disposal the compiler emits itself, so a disposal method of any other class would never be called ``
  (`tests/cases/reject_thread_dispose_elsewhere`).
- **There is no thread count.** Each spawn is one task and each task one
  thread; a scope with more tasks than cores leaves the scheduler to share them
  ([wp29-thread-surface.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp29-thread-surface.md) §9 declines the knob until
  a measurement asks for it).

What a task may do is what a data-parallel body may, less the rules about an
element's arena, which a task does not share, and each rule is reported at the
`spawn`:

- **The task writes nothing another can see**, except through the guard of a
  [`Mutex`](#a-lock-that-owns-its-data-mutext), the one shared write a task may
  make, by a method of an [atomic](#atomics-atomici32-and-atomici64)
  (`tests/link/thread_atomic_tasks`), or by a `send` or a receive on a
  [`Channel`](#channels-channelt), neither of which is a write the rule counts:
  `` `bump` writes memory its caller can see at main.ts:10:3, and `spawn` runs it beside the scope's other tasks: make scratch only this task uses inside it, because an object handed in as the argument is shared memory even when the `spawn` made it, since where an argument was made is not tracked. Write memory the tasks share only through the guard of a `Mutex`; hand a value the parent needs back as the task's answer, or run it on the thread that called it, `out[0] = bump(c)` ``
  (NL2471; `tests/cases/reject_thread_task_shared_write`, and
  `reject_mutex_task_unguarded` for a task that also writes through a guard).
  A `wipe` is a write through its argument like any other, so it is shared
  exactly when its target is: an array the task, or a function it calls,
  allocated itself is private, and wiping it is allowed
  (`tests/link/thread_task_wipe`). So is a `Secret` the function makes with
  `secret(v)` and wipes, when `v` is allocated in the call — `new`, an array
  literal or an object literal — and the `Secret` is held by a `const`
  (`tests/link/thread_task_wipe_secret`). Wiping the task's argument, a
  captured local, a field, an element, an array a call answered, a `Secret`
  held by a `let`, made from a call's answer, from a local moved into it or
  from a record whose constructor is handed an object, a `Secret` a call
  answers (wiped, or written by a helper first), or one a holder keeps in a
  field, is NL2471 (`reject_thread_wipe_param`, `_capture`, `_field`,
  `_element`, `_helper`, `_call_result`,
  `reject_thread_wipe_secret_call_result`, `_moved`, `_holder`, `_let`,
  `_call_secret`, `_call_secret_helper`, `_ctor_param`). A helper may write
  the task's own `Secret` before the wipe. A borrowed `Secret` parameter is
  refused before it
  (`reject_thread_wipe_secret_borrowed`). The wipe itself is unchanged, one
  volatile `llvm.memset`.
  A lookup in a shared `Map` or `Set` — `get`, `has`, `size` — is a read, so
  tasks of one scope may look keys up in the same table
  (`tests/link/thread_scope_task_map_reads`). A mutator — `set`, `add`,
  `delete`, `clear`, `getOrInsert` — writes it, a walk counts itself into it
  (`walkOpen`), and what a lookup answers is the table's memory, so each is
  refused (`reject_thread_task_map_set`, `_map_delete`, `_map_clear`,
  `_map_get_or_insert`, `_set_add`, `_set_delete`, `_set_clear`,
  `_map_walk_keys`, `_map_walk_values`, `_set_walk`, `_map_readback_write`).
  A task may `panic`, as a parallel body may: the first panic of the program
  prints and exits 1, and a task that panics after it prints nothing. Output
  stays a write (`reject_thread_task_console_error`,
  `reject_thread_task_process_exit`), and so does the parent's: between the
  first `spawn` and the join it may neither change a `Map` or `Set` it holds
  nor walk one — `for (const k of s)`, `m.keys()`, `m.values()`, or a helper
  that does (`reject_thread_region_parent_table_set`, `_set_walk`,
  `_map_keys_walk`, `_map_values_walk`, `_helper_walk`). The rule is
  conservative: it judges the call by what it writes through its receiver,
  not by which tables a task holds, so a walk of a table no task can reach is
  refused too (`reject_thread_region_parent_unreached_walk`), and so is a
  mutator or a walk called straight on a table made in the block. Proving
  that no task reaches one table would mean following every pointer each
  task is handed; the walk moves before the first `spawn`, after the block,
  or into a helper that makes and fills its own table
  (`thread_scope_region_own_tables`).
  A store into an array the task allocated and hands to nothing that keeps it
  is not counted, as for a [parallel body](#data-parallelism-nishthreads): a
  sieve may fill its own table, and a helper may fill the array it is handed
  (`tests/link/thread_task_private`). Returned, stored into its argument's
  field, pushed onto its argument's array, kept by a helper or a constructor,
  or bound to a second name in a later declarator, the array is shared
  (`tests/cases/reject_thread_task_private_returned`, `_field`, `_pushed`,
  `_kept`, `_new`, `_declarator`). A constructor that hands `this` out can
  lead to the array only by keeping it, so that route is `_new`'s. A store through a `?:` with the
  array in one arm is a store into either (`_ternary`), and an element of a
  private array of arrays is the array it holds
  (`reject_thread_task_private_nested`). The same holds for the task's other
  own memory: a method that writes only the fields of an object the task made,
  `const h = new Holder(); h.poke()`; `set`, `add` and `delete` on a `Map` or
  a `Set` it made; a store into an array field of an object it made, whose
  constructor filled it with a fresh array; a second name for its array bound
  in the same statement, `xs = new Array<i32>(n), ys = xs`; and a store
  through what a helper answers when the helper answers its argument, the
  task's own array, all write nothing shared
  (`tests/link/thread_task_own_writes`). What the argument reaches is not the
  task's own, even when the `spawn` made it there, because where an argument
  was made is not tracked: an object the task makes that holds the argument's
  array from its constructor on, has a field re-pointed at it, or is handed it
  by a helper or a method, and a helper that may answer either its own array
  or the caller's, all write the caller's memory
  (`reject_thread_task_own_holds_param`, `_repointed`, `_helper_stores_param`,
  `_method_adopts_param`, `_either_returned`), and so does a second name bound
  in the same statement as a fresh array when it names the argument's
  (`reject_thread_task_own_declarator_binds_arg`). A helper's fresh answer
  that holds the caller's memory, `[ys]` or `new H(ys)`, is the task's at its
  top level only, so a write below it is refused
  (`reject_thread_task_own_fresh_holds_array`, `_new`, `_object`). That
  refusal starts with what to write: `` make scratch only this task uses inside it, because an object handed in as the argument is shared memory even when the `spawn` made it, since where an argument was made is not tracked. Write memory the tasks share only through the guard of a `Mutex`; hand a value the parent needs back as the task's answer, or run it on the thread that called it, `out[0] = bump(c)` ``.
  A task inside a task, or
  inside a data-parallel body, is refused by this rule, because a scope's join
  stores into memory (`tests/cases/reject_thread_task_nested_spawn`); and a
  data-parallel call inside a task is refused by it too
  (`reject_thread_task_nested_map`).
- **It answers a number, a `boolean`, an enum, a `string`, or an array of
  numbers, booleans or enums**, because a task's thread frees its arena when it
  exits. A string or a scalar array crosses by copy-at-join: the worker copies
  its answer into a `malloc`'d transfer block before its arena goes
  (`nish_cross_out`), and the parent, once the scope has joined, copies each
  block into its own arena and frees it (`nish_cross_in`), so the block lives
  only between the two and is freed on every path out of the scope. An answer
  the task did not allocate — a literal, or a string its argument already held
  — passes through uncopied (`tests/link/thread_task_string`: a built label, a
  field of a made object, a substring and a slice, a returned fresh array, and
  a task that also stores into a `Mutex`, all read after `churn()`). Anything
  else is
  `` `words` answers `string[]`, and `spawn` hands back only a number, a `boolean`, an enum, a `string` or an array of numbers, booleans or enums, which the join copies out of the worker's arena: anything else would point into memory the worker frees or reuses ``
  (NL2348, `tests/cases/reject_thread_task_result_strings`;
  `reject_thread_task_result_type` for a class, `reject_thread_task_result_nested`
  for `i32[][]` and `reject_thread_task_result_map` for a `Map`). What a task
  allocates on the way is freed with its thread.
- **It leaves the arena alone**, because the first task runs in the arena of
  the thread that opened the scope:
  `` `wipe` reads or moves the arena, and `spawn` runs it on several threads that each have an arena of their own: a parallel body may not call `Arena.mark` or `Arena.used`, nor open a `using a = arena()` block, nor call `region`, `regionWith`, `child`, `childWith`, `enter`, `enterWith` or `free` (`nish:region`) ``
  (`tests/cases/reject_thread_task_arena`).
- **Its argument is not a `Result` small enough to travel as its parts**:
  `` The argument of `spawn` is `Result<i32, i32>`, which a task cannot be handed: a `Result` is passed as its parts rather than as one value, so hand the task the value it holds ``
  (`tests/cases/reject_thread_task_result_arg`).

Under Node, `scope()` is an object whose `spawn` runs its task at once and
stores the answer there; the rule above is what makes that print the same as
the compiled program ([RUN_UNDER_NODE.md](../../RUN_UNDER_NODE.md)). `using` needs
`--js-explicit-resource-management` on Node 22 and is native from Node 24.

`parallelFor`, non-scalar results and `scope(n)` are not in this stage
([wp29-thread-surface.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp29-thread-surface.md) §7); the lock is the next
section, [atomics](#atomics-atomici32-and-atomici64) the one after it, and
[channels](#channels-channelt) the one after that.

## A lock that owns its data: `Mutex<T>`

A `Mutex` lets a scope's tasks share one value they all update: the data lives
inside the lock, and the only way to it is the guard `lock()` answers, bound by
`using`, which holds the lock until its block ends
([wp29-thread-surface.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp29-thread-surface.md) §4.3). It is Rust's
`Mutex<T>`, narrowed until no borrow checker is needed.

```typescript
import { Mutex, scope } from "nish/threads";

class Counter {
  n: i32 = 0;
}

const addMany = (total: Mutex<Counter>): i32 => {
  for (let k: i32 = 0; k < 100000; k++) {
    using g = total.lock();          // waits for the lock, and holds it to the block's end
    g.value.n = g.value.n + 1;
  }                                  // released here, on every pass
  return 0;
};

export const main = (): i32 => {
  const total = new Mutex<Counter>(new Counter());
  const done: i32[] = [0, 0, 0, 0];
  {
    using s = scope();
    for (let t: i32 = 0; t < 4; t++) {
      s.spawn(addMany, total, done, t);
    }
  }
  using g = total.lock();
  console.log(`${g.value.n}`);       // 400000
  return 0;
};
```

- **Natively the lock is one word inside the guard**, taken with an acquire
  compare-and-swap in `lock()` and given back with a release store, so a lock
  nobody holds costs one atomic instruction and allocates nothing; a `lock()`
  that finds the word held calls the runtime's `nish_mutex_wait`, which spins
  briefly and then yields until it can take it (`tests/link/thread_mutex_counter`,
  whose `threads.ll` is the lowering, and `tests/link/thread_mutex_histogram`).
  On `wasm32` a scope's tasks run one after another, as they do for every
  scope there, so no lock is ever found held: the same program links for
  `--profile wasi`, its atomics lowered for a module without shared memory,
  and prints the same total (`tests/run.js`, "the `--profile wasi` build").
- **The release is emitted at every exit of the guard's block**: its end, a
  `break` or `continue` that leaves it, and a `return` or an `orReturn` — after
  the returned value is computed and before control leaves, unlike a scope's
  join, which runs before the value, so `return g.value.n` reads under the
  lock (`tests/link/thread_mutex_or_return`, whose `main.ll` pins the order) —
  and inside an `arena()` block it is given back before the arena releases
  (`tests/link/thread_mutex_exit_paths`, which locks again after each exit and
  would wait on itself if one kept the lock).

Eight rules keep every path to the data behind the lock, and a program that
breaks one is refused with that rule's own code:

- **R1: the data is fresh all the way down, and only the guard reaches it.**
  `new Mutex<T>(init)` takes a scalar, or a `new` expression or a literal whose
  every argument, element or value is a number, a `boolean`, an enum, a string
  literal — immutable, and never stored over — or itself fresh by this rule,
  because a value the program already holds would be a path to the data that
  skips the lock:
  `` `new Mutex` takes a value that is fresh all the way down — a `new` expression or a literal whose every argument or element is a number, a `boolean`, an enum, a string literal or itself fresh — because the data a `Mutex` owns is reachable only through its guard, and a value the program already holds would be a path to it that skips the lock ``
  (NL2463, `tests/cases/reject_mutex_not_fresh`,
  `reject_mutex_not_fresh_deep` for `new Hist(bins)` with a named `bins`, and
  `reject_mutex_not_fresh_literal` for `[row]` with a named `row`;
  `new Mutex<Label>(new Label("total", 0))` compiles,
  `tests/link/thread_mutex_scalar`). And `lock` is the only member
  of a `Mutex` a program may name:
  `` `guard` is not a member a program may name: the data a `Mutex` owns is reachable only through the guard its `lock()` answers, `using g = m.lock()`, so every path to it takes the lock ``
  (NL2464, `reject_mutex_member`).
- **R2: `m.lock()` is only the initialiser of a `using` declaration**, the
  third disposable beside `scope()` and `arena()`, and one `using` takes one
  lock (a second declarator's `lock()` is R5's, below). A lock may share a
  `using` with a scope opened before it or with an arena on either side, and
  the declarators close in the reverse of the order they opened, each opening
  before the next declarator's initialiser runs (an `orReturn()` there closes
  the ones before it), so in
  `using a = arena(), g = m.lock()` the lock is given back before the arena
  releases (`tests/link/thread_mutex_using_mixed`); a scope opened after the
  lock, `using g = m.lock(), s = scope()`, is R5's
  (`reject_mutex_using_lock_then_scope`). A `lock()` anywhere but a `using`
  initialiser is
  `` `lock()` must be the initialiser of a `using` declaration: the lock is released when the block that declares it ends, so a guard bound any other way would be one nobody releases; declare it as `using g = m.lock()` ``
  (NL2465, `reject_mutex_lock_not_using`; `reject_mutex_lock_expr_body` for
  an arrow whose expression body is `m.lock()`).
- **R3: a guard is used only as `g.value`, and what it reaches only as the base
  of another access.** Bound, stored, returned or walked, a guard is
  `` A guard is used only as `g.value`, and `g.value` only as the base of a field or element read or store: passed, bound, stored, returned or walked, what it reaches would outlive the block that holds the lock; write `g.value.n` where the value is used, or hand `g` to a helper whose parameter is a `MutexGuard<Counter>` ``
  (NL2466, `reject_mutex_guard_helper_return`, `reject_mutex_guard_helper_field`,
  `reject_mutex_guard_helper_ternary`). The one place a guard may go is to a
  **guard helper**: a function named at the call, neither a method, a
  constructor nor a generic, whose parameter in that position is declared as
  the guard is, `MutexGuard<T>`, with the guard named once among the call's
  arguments:

  ```ts
  const bump = (g: MutexGuard<Counter>): void => {
    g.value.n = g.value.n + 1;
  };

  {
    using g = m.lock();
    bump(g);
  }
  ```

  A guard helper is named, never held: naming it as a value is
  `` `bump` takes a `MutexGuard`: a guard is handed only to a function named at the call, so a function reference cannot name it; call the helper by name ``
  (NL2739, `reject_mutex_guard_helper_ternary_alias`,
  `reject_mutex_guard_helper_nullish`), because the rules below follow the
  function a call names.

  The helper's parameter is held to R3–R5 in its body exactly as `g` is in the
  block, so it can only read and store through it, and R5 follows the call, so
  a helper that locks, opens a scope, spawns or receives is refused at the call
  (`reject_mutex_guard_helper_spawn`, `reject_mutex_guard_helper_receive`). A
  helper that passes the guard on is judged by the same rule at that call
  (`reject_mutex_guard_helper_forward`), through helpers that call each other
  (`reject_mutex_guard_helper_mutual`) and across an import
  (`link/reject_mutex_guard_helper_import`); a helper that locks a `Mutex`
  it is handed is refused by R5 at the call
  (`reject_mutex_guard_helper_second_lock`), and `g.value` handed beside the
  guard by NL2467 (`reject_mutex_guard_helper_value_arg`). A helper has no
  default, rest or destructured parameter, which Nish has none of
  (`reject_mutex_guard_helper_default`, `_rest`, `_destructured`).
  `link/thread_mutex_helper` is three helpers deep on four threads. Any other call is
  `` `g` is passed to `push`, a method: a guard is handed only to a function named at the call, neither a method, a constructor nor a generic, whose parameter is declared as the guard is, `MutexGuard<T>`, once per call, because that parameter is held to the rules of the guard's block; write the helper as `const useGuard = (g: MutexGuard<Counter>): void => { console.log(g.value.n) }` and call it as `useGuard(g)` ``
  (NL2536; `reject_mutex_guard_helper_array`, `_map`, `_method`, `_new`,
  `_ctor_this`, `_generic`, `_twice`, `_nullable`, and `_callback` for a
  helper that takes a function, which makes it a generic), because a method or a
  constructor has `this` as a second way out, a generic's body treats `T` as any
  value, and a guard passed twice is two names for one lock. Anything read through it that is
  not a number, a `boolean`, an enum or a `string` — `const c = g.value`,
  `g.value.xs` as a value, a `for...of` over it — is
  `` This reads `Counter` through a guard, whose chains are only the base of a further field or element read or store: a value that is not a number, a `boolean`, an enum or a `string`, which the read copies, would outlive the block that holds the lock; do the work inside the guard's block, or read the numbers and strings it holds one at a time, `const n = g.value.n` ``
  (NL2467, `reject_mutex_guard_alias`; `reject_mutex_guard_alias_array` for
  `const b = g.value.bins`, which would race a guarded write once the block
  ends; `reject_mutex_guard_return` and `reject_mutex_guard_return_array` for a
  return; `reject_mutex_guard_store_field` and `reject_mutex_guard_store_element`
  for a store; `reject_mutex_guard_for_of` for a walk). An arrow's expression
  body is its answer and is judged as a `return` of it is, so a helper written
  `(g: MutexGuard<Box>): Box => g.value` is refused as one that writes
  `return g.value` (`reject_mutex_guard_helper_expr_value`, `_field`, `_paren`,
  `_index`, `link/reject_mutex_guard_helper_expr_import`; `_call`, `_new` and
  `_cond` for `g.value` handed to a call or a `new`, or written as an arm of
  `? :`, inside the body), and
  `reject_mutex_guard_helper_expr_churn` is the use-after-free it would open: the
  object kept past the lock, its string replaced under a second lock, and
  `churn()` reusing the memory before the old one is printed. An arrow argument,
  which may read its function's `const` locals, may not read a guard among
  them, whether it runs on this thread (`reject_mutex_guard_capture`) or is
  passed to a data-parallel form (`reject_par_capture_guard`). A scalar read through the guard is a value like any other, `.length`
  of an array it reaches included. When `T` is itself a scalar, `g.value` is
  read and stored directly — `g.value = g.value + 1` on a `Mutex<i32>` — and
  the store reaches the `Mutex` under Node as natively, because the guard is
  the `Mutex`'s own storage rather than a copy (`tests/link/thread_mutex_scalar`).
- **R4: a store through a guard stores a scalar or a string, and no method is
  called through it.** A number, a `boolean`, an enum or a `string`, into a
  field or an element of an array that already exists:
  `` This stores `string[]` through a guard, which stores only a number, a `boolean`, an enum or a `string`, which the store copies, into a field or an element that already exists: anything else is a pointer, which may point into a task's arena, freed when the task is joined; build the value into the one the `Mutex` is made with, or store what it holds one at a time into slots that already exist, `g.value.names[i] = v[i]` ``
