  (NL2468, `reject_mutex_guard_store`; `reject_mutex_guard_store_class` for a
  class). A `null` is stored through a guard only into a `string | null` slot —
  a field, an element or a `Mutex<string | null>` — where the store frees the
  copy the slot held and keeps nothing, so a later read through `?.` answers
  `null` (`tests/link/thread_mutex_null_store`, natively and under Node, read
  back after `churn()`). Into any other nullable slot, a `Link | null` field,
  element or `Mutex<Link | null>`, it is refused, since such a slot holds a
  pointer, which a guard stores in no form:
  `` This stores `null` through a guard into a slot that holds an object, and a guard stores only a number, a `boolean`, an enum or a `string`, and a `null` only into a `string | null` slot, where the store frees the copy the slot held; keep a `boolean` field beside the slot, `g.value.hasNext = false`, and test it before reading the object ``
  (NL2537, `reject_mutex_guard_null_class`, `_link_element`, `_link_value`,
  `_link_nested` for `g.value.inner.next = null`, and `_link_paren` for
  `g.value.next = (null)`). Only the literal `null` is stored: a
  `string | null` *value*, a variable or a `??`, is refused as NL2468 above,
  since the store copies what it is given and a value that may be `null` would
  need a test the store does not make. A string stored through a guard is copied into memory the mutex
  owns: `nish_guard_keep` `malloc`s the copy, records it, and frees the copy
  the slot held before, if that one was its own; a string read through a guard
  is copied out into the reader's arena (`.length` excepted, which keeps
  nothing), so no reader holds the block the next store frees. The block a
  slot holds when the `Mutex` itself is dropped is not freed — the arena that
  held the `Mutex` does not say when it goes — and is reported by valgrind as
  still reachable, one block per guarded string slot
  (`tests/link/thread_mutex_string`). A program that makes and drops many such
  `Mutex`es keeps all of them: 100,000, each holding one 850-byte string,
  peaked at 89 MB against 11 MB for the same loop without the store. The
  record of those copies is one for the process, behind a lock of its own, so
  stores through two different `Mutex`es wait on each other while it is held.
  `push` — which can move the array into the task's arena — and every other
  method are
  `` `push` is called through a guard, which reads and stores fields and elements and calls no method: a method could keep what it reaches, or grow an array into a task's arena, which is freed when it is joined; write what it does as reads and stores through the guard, into slots that already exist, `g.value.xs[0] = 1` ``
  (NL2469, `reject_mutex_guard_push`). So a `Mutex<i32[]>` or a class with an
  `i32[]` field holds a histogram, sized when it is made.
- **R5: one lock at a time, and nothing waited on while it is held.** Inside a
  guard's block — directly, or through any function it calls — a second
  `lock()`, `scope()`, `spawn`, `parallelMapInto` or `parallelReduce` is
  `` A second `lock()` is reached while `ga` holds its lock: inside a guard's block, directly or through any function it calls, there is no second `lock()`, no `scope()` or `spawn`, and no `parallelMapInto` or `parallelReduce`, so one lock is held at a time and nothing is waited on while it is held; move `b.lock()` below the end of the block that opens with `using ga = a.lock()`, which releases the lock ``
  (NL2470; `reject_mutex_nested_lock`, and `reject_mutex_using_two_locks` and
  `reject_mutex_using_two_mutexes` for a second declarator of the same `using`;
  `reject_mutex_lock_through_call` for a callee that locks, and
  `reject_mutex_held_new` for a constructor that does, reached by `new`;
  `reject_mutex_held_scope` and `reject_mutex_held_scope_call` for a scope;
  `reject_mutex_held_map` and `reject_mutex_held_reduce` for the data-parallel
  calls). That is the whole
  argument that **a program cannot deadlock**: a task holding a lock never
  waits for anything, so every lock is given back.
- **R6: a store through a guard is the one shared write a task may make.** P2's
  rule is otherwise unchanged (above, NL2471).
- **R7: from the statement that holds a scope's first `spawn` to the end of
  its block, the parent does not lock what the scope's tasks share**, directly
  or through any function or constructor it calls — P2's own window, so a lock
  before the `spawn` in the same loop body is inside it: on the loop's second
  pass that lock runs after the first pass's `spawn`
  (`reject_mutex_region_lock_loop`).
  Natively the tasks have not run yet there, and under Node each has run at its
  spawn, so the parent would see a different value:
  `` This `lock()` locks a `Mutex` a task of `s` can reach through `arg`, before the scope joins: natively the scope's tasks run when its block ends and under Node each runs where it is spawned, so the parent locks what they share only before the statement that holds the first `spawn` or after the join; move `m.lock()` above the block that opens with `using s = scope()`, or below the end of that block ``
  (NL2472, `reject_mutex_region_lock`; `reject_mutex_region_lock_field` for a
  `Mutex` the task reaches as a field of its argument;
  `reject_mutex_region_lock_call` for a call that takes the lock, and
  `reject_mutex_region_lock_new` for a `new` whose constructor does). It is asked by type: a `Mutex<T>` of the
  type a task's argument reaches, or, for a call that takes a lock, any
  `Mutex` a task reaches. Before the first `spawn` and after the join the
  parent locks freely, as `tests/link/thread_mutex_counter` does.
- **R8: a `Mutex` reaches a task as its argument, or as a field of the class
  its argument is.** An array of them, a deeper field, or a `Mutex` inside
  another's data is
  `` The argument of `spawn` is `Mutex<Counter>[]`, which reaches a `Mutex` through `ms[i]`: a `Mutex` reaches a task as its argument or as a field of the class its argument is, never deeper, so which tasks share a lock is a question the checker can answer; hand the task the `Mutex` itself, `s.spawn(first, ms[i], done, 0)`, and declare its parameter a `Mutex` of the same data ``
  (NL2473, `reject_mutex_task_array`; `reject_mutex_task_nested` for a `Mutex`
  inside another's data, `reject_mutex_task_deep` for one two classes deep,
  `reject_mutex_task_nullable` for a nullable carrier, `reject_mutex_task_map`
  for a `Map` holding them). A task's destination holds numbers, so a
  `Mutex` is never one.

And a lock is a scope's: the body of `parallelMapInto` or `parallelReduce`,
which runs on many threads at once, takes none
(`` `tally` takes a `Mutex`'s lock, and `parallelMapInto` runs it on several threads at once: a lock is taken by a scope's task or by the thread that opened the scope, never by a parallel body; run it as a scope's tasks instead, `{ using s2 = scope(); for (let i = 0; i < src.length; i++) { s2.spawn(tally, src[i], dst, i) } }` ``,
NL2474, `reject_mutex_parallel_body`; `reject_mutex_parallel_body_call` and
`reject_mutex_parallel_body_new` for a lock taken in a callee or a
constructor).

**What a guarded program means.** The tasks' critical sections run one at a
time, in some order. Natively the order is the scheduler's; under Node, where
`lock()` answers the guard at once and its `[Symbol.dispose]` does nothing, it
is spawn order, which is one of the native orders
([RUN_UNDER_NODE.md](../../RUN_UNDER_NODE.md)). A program prints the same both ways
when its guarded updates commute exactly — integer sums and counts, a minimum,
a histogram; an `f64` sum does not, because the order changes its bits — and
no task's answer or control flow depends on guarded state it read. Anything
else is its author's obligation, as an associative operator is for a named
function given to `parallelReduce`; the checker does not try to prove it. It
is the one place the lock weakens the scope's promise above, that the checker
refuses anything that could tell the two orders apart.

## Atomics: `AtomicI32` and `AtomicI64`

An atomic is one integer a scope's tasks, and the bodies of the data-parallel
forms, update at once without a lock: each method is a single indivisible
operation on the word, so no update is lost to a race and none waits for
another. Where a `Mutex` guards a whole value, an atomic guards one counter.
The fast way to use one is the example's: each task counts into a local tally
no other core touches and adds it to the shared counters once, at its end, so
the atomics see one update per bin per task rather than one per value
("Measured", below).

```typescript
import { AtomicI32, parallelMapInto, scope } from "nish/threads";

class Shard {
  xs: i32[];
  bins: AtomicI32[];
  constructor(xs: i32[], bins: AtomicI32[]) {
    this.xs = xs;
    this.bins = bins;
  }
}

const binShard = (s: Shard): i32 => {
  const local: i32[] = [0, 0, 0, 0]; // this task's own counts: no core shares them
  for (const x of s.xs) {
    const bin: i32 = x & 3;
    if (bin < local.length) {
      local[bin] += 1;
    }
  }
  for (let b = 0; b < local.length; b++) {
    s.bins[b].add(local[b]);         // one indivisible add per bin, no lock
  }
  return 0;
};

export const main = (): i32 => {
  const bins: AtomicI32[] = [new AtomicI32(0), new AtomicI32(0), new AtomicI32(0), new AtomicI32(0)];
  const done: i32[] = [0, 0];
  {
    using s = scope();
    s.spawn(binShard, new Shard([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], bins), done, 0);
    s.spawn(binShard, new Shard([6, 7, 8], bins), done, 1);
  }
  const big = new AtomicI32(0);
  const xs: i32[] = [3, 9, 4];
  const ys: i32[] = [0, 0, 0];
  parallelMapInto(xs, ys, (x) => big.max(x));  // the one shared write a body may make
  console.log(`${bins[0].load()} ${bins[1].load()} ${big.load()}`); // 2 2 9
  return 0;
};
```

- **The methods.** `load()` and `store(v)`; `add(n)`, `sub(n)`, `min(v)`,
  `max(v)` and `exchange(v)`, each answering the value the word held before
  it; and `compareExchange(expected, desired)`, which stores `desired` when the
  word holds `expected` and answers the value it saw either way, so a loop
  that retries until the answer is its `expected` builds any other update
  (`tests/link/thread_atomic_tasks`). `add` and `sub` wrap at the width;
  `min` and `max` compare signed. `AtomicI64` is the same over `i64`.
- **Natively each method is one instruction**, sequentially consistent: a
  `load atomic` or `store atomic ... seq_cst`, an `atomicrmw add`, `sub`,
  `min`, `max` or `xchg ... seq_cst`, or a `cmpxchg ... seq_cst seq_cst`,
  aligned to the width (`align 4`, `align 8`), the whole body of the method's
  instance in `nish/threads`'s module (`tests/link/thread_atomic_tasks`, whose
  `threads.ll` is the lowering; docs/IR_COOKBOOK.md, "an atomic"). On
  `wasm32` a scope's tasks and a parallel call's chunks run one after another,
  and the same IR is lowered for a module without shared memory.
- **Under Node each method is the plain operation** on an ordinary field,
  which is exact because Node runs every task at its `spawn` and every parallel
  body in order. Node holds an `AtomicI64` as a `number`, and it agrees with
  native while values stay within ±2^53; wrapping at 2^63 is native-only, the
  same limit as every `i64` ([RUN_UNDER_NODE.md](../../RUN_UNDER_NODE.md)), so a
  program meant to run under Node as well passes it `i64`-typed values, not
  `toI64` of a number, which is a BigInt there.

Three rules keep every touch of the word indivisible and every program's
answer the same natively and under Node:

- **R1: an atomic is reached only by calling its methods.** Its word is a
  field, `value`, that no program may name, read or store:
  `` `value` is not a member a program may name: an atomic is read and updated only by calling its methods, `load()`, `add(n)` and the rest, each one indivisible: a plain read or store of its word would race with the update a task makes at the same moment ``
  (NL2514, `tests/cases/reject_atomic_member_read`, `reject_atomic_member_store`,
  and `reject_atomic_member_nested` for `h.a.b.value`). A method named without
  a call is refused by the rule every class's methods keep, not by NL2514:
  `` Unknown field `add` on class `AtomicI64` (it is a method; call it) ``
  (`reject_atomic_member_unbound`). `new AtomicI32(v)` takes a number, so an
  atomic is fresh when it is made, and `new` is the only way one is made. An
  object literal of any class of `nish/threads` — an atomic, a `Mutex`, its
  `MutexGuard`, a `Channel` or a `ThreadScope` — would be a plain record under
  Node, without the methods, and is refused with
  `` `AtomicI32` is a class of `nish/threads`, and its objects are made only as the module makes them: `new AtomicI32(v)`, `new AtomicI64(v)`, `new Mutex(v)`, `new Channel()`, `m.lock()` and `scope()`. An object literal would be a plain record under Node, with none of the methods the class is used through ``
  (NL2515, `tests/cases/reject_atomic_literal`, `reject_atomic_literal_i64`,
  `reject_thread_literal_channel`, `reject_thread_literal_mutex` and
  `reject_thread_literal_mutex_only`, whose `Mutex` literal is refused by this
  rule rather than by `new Mutex`'s fresh-value one, and
  `reject_thread_literal_scope`).
- **R7: from the statement that holds a scope's first `spawn` to the end of its
  block, the parent does not touch an atomic the scope's tasks can reach** —
  with a method, or through any function, method or constructor it calls,
  or by a data-parallel call that does — `Mutex`'s R7, for the same reason:
  natively the tasks have not run there, and under Node each has run at its
  spawn, so a `load()` would answer differently:
  `` This `load()` reaches an atomic a task of `s` can reach through `arg`, before the scope joins: natively the scope's tasks run when its block ends and under Node each runs where it is spawned, so the parent touches what they share only before the statement that holds the first `spawn` or after the join; move `a.load()` above the block that opens with `using s = scope()`, or below the end of that block ``
  (NL2513, `reject_atomic_region_direct`; `reject_atomic_region_capture` for
  an arrow task that captures it; `reject_atomic_region_field`,
  `reject_atomic_region_array`, `reject_atomic_region_map` and
  `reject_atomic_region_generic` for one the task's argument reaches through a
  field, an element, a `Map`'s value or a generic's field;
  `reject_atomic_region_call`, `reject_atomic_region_method` and
  `reject_atomic_region_new` for a function, a method and a constructor that
  touch it; `reject_atomic_region_this` for one reached through `this` handed
  out of a constructor; `reject_atomic_region_declarators` for the second
  declarator of a declaration; `reject_atomic_region_spawn_arg` for a second
  `spawn`'s argument; `reject_atomic_region_parallel` for a parallel call).
  It is asked by type, as `Mutex`'s is: an atomic of the type a task's argument
  or capture reaches, at any depth, so an alias through `?:` or a function's
  answer is the same atomic (`reject_atomic_region_ternary`,
  `reject_atomic_region_return`), and so is any other atomic of that type the
  task cannot in fact reach. An atomic of a type no task reaches is the
  parent's alone, and its methods are not counted as writes the scope's tasks
  may read (`tests/link/thread_atomic_unreached`). Before the first `spawn` and
  after the join the parent touches it freely.

  The scopes of one `using` are judged against each other too: natively they
  join in reverse order, so a task of `t` in `using s = scope(), t = scope()`
  runs before every task of `s`, and under Node each runs at its spawn. A
  `spawn` on one of them whose task shares a destination, an atomic or a lock
  with a task of another scope of the same statement is refused, naming the
  other scope and the path it shares:
  `` This `spawn` on `t` hands its task an atomic through `a`, which a task of `s` also reaches: the scopes one `using` statement opens join one after the other natively, the last declared first, while under Node each task runs where it is spawned, so the tasks of sibling scopes share no lock, no atomic and no destination; open each scope in a block of its own, so the first joins before the second opens, `{ using s = scope(); s.spawn(() => { a.add(1); }) } { using t = scope(); t.spawn(() => { b.store(a.load()); }) }` ``
  (NL2516). A destination is shared when two scopes' spawns name the same
  array, at the same slot or at different ones
  (`reject_thread_sibling_destination`, `_slots`, `_arrow` for arrow tasks,
  `_three` for three declarators). A task that reaches another scope's
  destination — to read the answer that scope's task returns, or to write it —
  hands the array on, which the destination rule refuses before this one:
  `_void` writes it, `_read` reads it through an arrow's capture, `_new`
  through a constructor reached by `new`, and `_this` through a field of an
  object whose constructor hands `this` out. An atomic or a lock is told apart by the `const` it was made in by
  `new`: a task handed that binding, as its argument or a capture, reaches that
  object and no other, and two such bindings are two objects. Reached any other
  way — through another binding, a field, an element, a function's answer —
  it is read as any object of its type, which meets every one
  (`reject_atomic_sibling_load`, `reject_atomic_sibling_exchange`,
  `reject_atomic_sibling_arrow`, `reject_atomic_sibling_three`,
  `reject_thread_mutex_sibling`, `reject_thread_mutex_sibling_alias` for a
  second name of one lock, `reject_thread_mutex_sibling_field` for one reached
  through a field). Every way a task reaches the object counts: through a
  field of a field (`reject_atomic_sibling_field_field`,
  `reject_thread_mutex_sibling_field_field`), through an object whose
  constructor hands `this` out (`reject_atomic_sibling_this`,
  `reject_thread_mutex_sibling_this`), in a constructor reached by `new`
  (`reject_atomic_sibling_new`, `reject_thread_mutex_sibling_new`), in a
  helper the task calls (`reject_atomic_sibling_helper`,
  `reject_thread_mutex_sibling_helper`), from an arrow's capture
  (`reject_thread_mutex_sibling_arrow`), and between any two declarators of
  the statement (`reject_thread_mutex_sibling_three`). Tasks that take no lock share none, and tasks that call no
  atomic method share no atomic. Sibling scopes whose tasks reach disjoint
  locks or atomics, of one type or of two, run as before
  (`tests/link/thread_sibling_disjoint_mutex`, `_mutex_types`, `_atomics`).
- **R8: an atomic reaches a task at any depth** — as its argument, a field of
  it, an element of an `AtomicI32[]`, or a capture — unlike a `Mutex`, which
  stops one field down: an atomic holds no data a task could keep, so which
  tasks share it is a question R7 answers by type, without the exact sharing
  set a lock's R5 needs.

**An atomic update is the one shared write a task or a parallel body may make
beside a guard.** A task that calls `add` on an atomic its argument reaches
writes nothing the rule above counts, and neither does the body of
`parallelMapInto`, `parallelMap`, `parallelFrom` or `parallelReduce`, which
takes no lock but may update an atomic it captures or an element reaches
(`tests/link/par_atomic`). Any other write beside it is refused as before
(`reject_atomic_par_shared_write`). A parallel body answers a number, never
an atomic (`reject_atomic_par_result`).

**What an atomic program means.** The updates land in some order: natively
the scheduler's, under Node spawn order and element order. A program prints
the same both ways when its updates commute exactly — `add` and `sub`, `min`,
`max`, a count, a histogram — and no task's answer or control flow depends on
a value it read from a word another task updates. A `store`, an `exchange` or a
`compareExchange` that wins against another task is order-dependent. A
`parallelReduce`'s blocks depend on `n` alone, the same on one core or sixty
four, but natively they run at once and under Node one after another, so what
a body does to an atomic must not depend on which block reaches it first. That is the
author's obligation, as it is for a `Mutex`'s critical sections; the checker
does not try to prove it.

**Measured.** `examples/histogram-atomic.ts` bins 4 × 2,000,000 values per
round into 256 bins, four rounds, on four tasks. On a four-core machine, over
seven interleaved rounds whose seeds move every round, the medians are: each
task counting into a local tally and adding it with one `add` per bin, 24 ms
(a byte-identical copy of it, the noise band, 24 ms, its runs 23–37 ms); one
thread binning into plain counters, 77 ms (3.2× slower); one atomic `add` per
value, 677 ms (28× slower), because every increment contends for a cache line
another core is writing; and one `Mutex` taken per value, 6,565 ms. An atomic
is far cheaper than a lock and still far dearer than a counter no other core
touches: update it once per batch, not once per value.

## Channels: `Channel<T>`

A `Channel` passes scalars from a scope's tasks to one receiver: the tasks that
produce call `send`, and the one that consumes walks the channel with
`for...of`, which waits for values and ends once every task that may send on
it has returned and it is drained
([wp29-thread-surface.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp29-thread-surface.md) §4.4). Nobody closes a
channel, so nobody can close one too early, or twice.

```typescript
import { Channel, scope } from "nish/threads";

class Pipe {
  ch: Channel<i32>;
  n: i32;
  constructor(ch: Channel<i32>, n: i32) {
    this.ch = ch;
    this.n = n;
  }
}

const produce = (p: Pipe): i32 => {
  for (let i: i32 = 1; i <= p.n; i++) {
    p.ch.send(i);                                 // never waits
  }
  return p.n;
};

const consume = (p: Pipe): i32 => {
  let sum: i32 = 0;
  for (const x of p.ch) {                         // waits; ends once the sender has returned
    sum = sum + x;
  }
  return sum;
};

export const main = (): i32 => {
  const sent: i32[] = [0];
  const sums: i32[] = [0];
  const ch = new Channel<i32>();                  // for one run of the scope below
  {
    using s = scope();
    s.spawn(produce, new Pipe(ch, 100), sent, 0); // every sender first
    s.spawn(consume, new Pipe(ch, 0), sums, 0);   // then the one receiver
  }
  console.log(`${sums[0]}`);                      // 5050
  return 0;
};
```

- **Natively a channel is a buffer of 8-byte slots outside every arena**, behind
  the channel's `state` word, with a lock, a condition to wait on and a count
  that keeps it open (runtime/runtime-parallel.c). `send` widens the value into
  a slot and never waits; the loop takes a slot and narrows it back, and waits
  while the channel is empty and open. The count starts at one for the scope:
  a `spawn` whose task may send on the channel adds one before the task is
  filed and takes it away when the task returns, and the scope takes its own
  away at every exit of its block, just before the join — whether or not the
  join finds a task to run — so a channel whose only sender was never spawned
  closes too (`tests/link/thread_channel_pipeline`, whose `main.ll` and
  `threads.ll` are the lowering; `tests/link/thread_channel_exit_paths` for the
  end of the block, a `return`, a `break` and a scope that runs nothing). On
  `wasm32` a scope's tasks run one after another in spawn order, every sender
  before the receiver, and the same programs print the same thing
  (`tests/run.js`, "the `--profile wasi` build").
- **The buffer is given back when a loop drains the channel closed**, and the
  channel records that, so a second loop over it ends at once rather than
  reading what was freed; a loop that stops early with `break` leaves the rest
  for the next one (`tests/link/thread_channel_parent_drain`). Only that drain
  gives anything back. A channel whose last loop stopped early with `break` or
  `return`, or that no loop ever walks, keeps its bookkeeping — a few dozen
  bytes for its lock, its count and its buffer's bounds — and the values left
  in its buffer until the program exits, one such allocation per run of the
  declaration.
- **Under Node a channel is an array queue.** `send` pushes, and the loop takes
  values off the front as it walks, so a second loop finds what the first left
  ([RUN_UNDER_NODE.md](../../RUN_UNDER_NODE.md)). That is correct because a task runs
  at its spawn under Node and every sender is spawned before the receiver, so
  every value has been sent by the time the receiver's loop starts.

Seven rules keep "every sender has returned" a single moment and the one
receiver from waiting on what never comes, and a program that breaks one is
refused with a code of that rule's own: ten codes, NL2475 to NL2484, because
C2 has one for where a channel is declared, one for how it is used and one for
a channel inside an arrow, and C6 one for spawn order and one for a task that
sends and receives:

- **C1: a channel carries a number, a `boolean`, an enum or a `string`.** A
  sender's arena is freed when its scope joins, so a string is copied on the
  way: `send` copies it into a `malloc`'d block the buffer slot holds
  (`nish_cross_send`, a copy in time that grows with the string alone:
  `tests/link/thread_channel_string_many` sends a million it also keeps), and
  `receive`, or a `for...of` step, copies it into the receiver's arena and frees the block (`nish_cross_in`). A string a receiver
  never takes — the loop that left with `break` — stays in the buffer, which
  is itself given back only once it has been drained closed, so the two leak
  together. Anything else would be a pointer into the sender's arena:
  `` A `Channel` carries a number, a `boolean`, an enum or a `string`, and this one would carry `string[]`: a sender's arena is freed when its scope joins, and only a string is copied out of it on the way, so anything else would point into freed memory; keep the values in an array the receiver can read and send each one's index, `const words = new Channel<i32>()` ``
  (NL2475, `tests/cases/reject_channel_element`). A `Channel<string>`
  pipeline — two producers, a rewriting stage and a consumer that keeps what
  it receives in an array — matches Node (`tests/link/thread_channel_string`). An `f64` channel
  (`tests/link/thread_channel_two_producers`), a `boolean` one
  (`thread_channel_parent_drain`), and an `i64`, an enum and a `u8` one
  (`thread_channel_kinds`) compile and carry their values exactly.
- **C2: a channel is a `const` declared beside its scope, and used only as a
  channel.** `new Channel<T>()` initialises a `const` in the block that holds
  the scope's `using s = scope()`, or in the block that has the scope's block
  as one of its statements, before it, with no loop, condition or function
  between, so each run of the declaration makes a channel for one run of one
  scope — a scope in a loop gets a fresh one every pass:
  `` `new Channel` must be the initialiser of a `const`: a channel is a `const` declared in the block that holds its scope's `using s = scope()`, or in the block that has the scope's block as one of its statements, before it, so each run of the declaration makes a channel for one run of one scope; write `const ch = new Channel<i32>()` on the line before `using s = scope()` ``
  (NL2476, `reject_channel_not_const`, `reject_channel_let_second_declarator`
  for a `let` that declares it beside something else, `reject_channel_scope_conditional`
  for a scope inside an `if`, and `reject_channel_scope_loop` for one inside a
  loop the declaration is outside; a function boundary between them is C4's,
  below). A channel is the receiver of `send`, the
  iterable of a `for...of`, an argument, or a field its class's constructor
  sets from a parameter — never bound to another name, stored, returned or
  compared, and no member but `send` is named:
  `` A `Channel` cannot be bound, stored, returned or compared here: a channel is used only as the receiver of `send`, the iterable of a `for...of`, an argument, or a field its class's constructor sets from a parameter, so it is never bound, stored, returned or captured, and which tasks reach it is a question the checker can answer ``
  (NL2477, `reject_channel_bound`, `reject_channel_member`, `reject_channel_member_take`, `_ready`,
  `_head` and `_state`, `reject_channel_returned_expr` for an arrow whose
  expression body is a channel, which is its answer, and `reject_channel_stored` for a class that holds one
  made anywhere but at the `spawn`; `reject_channel_nullable` for a task's
  argument whose channel may be `null`, which the `spawn` could not count as a
  sender). A type holds a channel only as exactly `Channel<T>`: never as one
  that may be `null`, an array's element, a `Result`'s arm or another
  generic's type argument, wherever the type is written — a local, a
  parameter, a result or a field, a type alias read as the type it names
  (`reject_channel_nullable`, `reject_channel_array`, `reject_channel_map_value`,
  `reject_channel_result_type`, `reject_channel_alias_type`,
  `reject_channel_field_generic`). An argument is one only
  to a parameter its function declares a `Channel`, not to a generic's `T`
  (`reject_channel_generic_argument`). It reaches a task as R8 says a `Mutex`
  does: as the task's argument, or as a field of the object made for it at the
  `spawn`, `new Pipe(ch, 100)`, and by one path only, so a task never holds it
  in two fields (`reject_channel_two_paths`). A constructor uses a channel it
  is handed only to set a field from it, `this.ch = ch` (`reject_channel_ctor_bound`);
  one it declares itself it uses as any function does. And a channel is used
  only in a top-level function's own body, never inside an arrow, which is
  lifted into a function of its own that these rules do not follow:
  `` A `Channel` is used inside an arrow here: an arrow is lifted into a function of its own that the channel rules do not follow, so a channel is declared, sent on and received from only in a top-level function's own body; write the arrow as a module function, `const relayBody = (q: Pipe): i32 => { const c = q.ch; c.send(1); return 1; }`, and pass `relayBody` where the arrow was ``
  (NL2484, `reject_channel_arrow`, and `reject_channel_arrow_nullable` for a
  channel type an arrow writes but never uses).
- **C3: a channel is unbounded**, so `send` never waits, because under Node a
  scope's tasks run one at a time and nothing would drain a full one:
  `` `new Channel` takes no capacity: a channel is unbounded and `send` never waits, because under Node a scope's tasks run one at a time and nothing would drain a channel that was full; write `new Channel<i32>()` ``
  (NL2478, `reject_channel_capacity`).
- **C4: one scope's tasks reach a channel, and the parent sends on it only
  before that scope's block.** After the join it only receives. "May send" is
  the call graph from a task's entry reaching `send` on a channel its argument
  holds, so an over-count only closes the channel later:
  `` This sends on `ch` once its scope's block has begun: a channel is reachable from the tasks of one scope, the parent sends on it only before the block that holds that scope's spawns, and nobody closes it: it closes once the scope has started to join and every task that may send on it has returned; move `ch.send(7)` above the block that opens with `using s = scope()` ``
  (NL2479, `reject_channel_parent_send`, `reject_channel_send_after_join` for a
  send through a call after the join, and `reject_channel_two_scopes` for the
  two scopes of one `using`). A `spawn` hands its task only a channel the
  function declared, never one it was handed, so no function boundary comes
  between a channel and its scope (`reject_channel_spawn_handed`, and
  `reject_channel_spawn_handed_direct` for the channel as the argument itself).
  In the constructor of a class that holds a channel, directly or through a
  field's class, `this` appears only as the base of its own field, `this.f`,
  used in one of three ways: as the target of a store (`this.f = ...`,
  `this.f += ...`); as any value, except as the callee of a call, when the field is a
  number, a `boolean`, an enum, a string or an array of those, from which
  nothing reaches a channel (`this.total = this.a + this.b`,
  `this.width = this.name.length`, `this.items.push(x)`); or as the base of a
  store into a field or element of what it holds, when that is no channel and
  holds none (`this.span.lo = 1`; `tests/link/thread_channel_ctor_reads`). A
  method called on it, an argument (to a function or to a constructor), a store
  elsewhere, a second name (in any declarator), an array element, a read of the
  channel or of an object that holds one, or `this` stored even into its own
  field would carry a send the count would not see:
  `` The constructor of a class that holds a channel uses `this` other than to read or set its own fields, `this.f`, where a send made through it could not be counted: … ``
  (NL2479; `reject_channel_ctor_this`, `reject_channel_ctor_this_stored`,
  `reject_channel_ctor_this_bound`, `reject_channel_ctor_this_array`,
  `reject_channel_ctor_this_new`, `reject_channel_ctor_this_declarator`,
  `reject_channel_ctor_this_self`, `reject_channel_ctor_this_deep_carrier`,
  `reject_channel_ctor_this_send`, `reject_channel_ctor_this_carrier`).
- **C5: a channel has one receiver** — one task, from a `spawn` outside any
  loop, or the parent in a later statement of the block that has the scope's
  block as one of its statements, never both — and inside a scope's block the
  parent receives nothing, directly or through any function it calls, so its
  one wait is the join:
  `` `ch` has a second receiver here: a channel has one receiver, either one task spawned outside any loop or the parent in a later statement of the block that has the scope's block as one of its statements, and inside a scope's block the parent receives nothing, so the parent's one wait is the join ``
  (NL2480, `reject_channel_two_receivers`, `reject_channel_parent_and_task`,
  `reject_channel_receiver_loop`, `reject_channel_parent_receive_inside` for a
  call that receives inside the block, `reject_channel_receive_in_spawn_argument`
  for one in a `spawn`'s argument, which is the parent's code, and
  `reject_channel_receive_before_using` for one before the `using` in the
  scope's own block). A call counts as a receive when its function may receive
  on a channel it is handed; one that receives only on a channel of its own has
  joined that channel's scope first, and is not one. One receiver is what makes
  "the receiver sees every value sent" true natively and under Node alike.
- **C6: every task that may send on a channel is spawned before the one that
  receives on it**, in the block's statement order. Under Node a receiver
  spawned first would find the channel empty, and the same order makes the
  graph from senders to receivers acyclic, so **channels cannot deadlock**
  either:
  `` `produce` may send on `ch` and is spawned after its receiver: under Node a task runs where it is spawned, so every task that may send on a channel is spawned, in the block's statement order, before the one task that receives on it, which is also what keeps channels from deadlocking; move the `spawn` of the receiving task below every `spawn` that sends, `s.spawn(produce, new Pipe(ch, 3), out, 1)` above `s.spawn(consume, new Pipe(ch, 0), out, 0)` ``
  (NL2481, `reject_channel_receiver_first`). And no task both sends and
  receives on one channel:
  `` `echo` may both send and receive on `ch`: no task both sends and receives on one channel, because a channel closes only once every task that may send on it has returned, and this one would wait in its own loop for its own return; split it into a task that sends and a task that receives, or answer the result through a second channel ``
  (NL2483, `reject_channel_send_and_receive`,
  `reject_channel_both_through_new` for a send made by a constructor a `new`
  runs, and `reject_channel_both_untraceable` for a task that reaches a
  channel through a second name for what holds it, which counts as using
  every channel it holds, and says so).
- **C7: nothing receives while a lock is held**, directly or through any
  function it calls — R5's "nothing is waited on while it is held". A `send`
  never waits and may stay:
  `` A loop over a channel is reached while `g` holds its lock: a receive waits, and nothing waits while a lock is held, so there is no receive inside a guard's block, directly or through any function it calls (a `send` never waits, and may stay) ``
  (NL2482, `reject_channel_loop_held`, and `reject_channel_receive_held_call`
  for a function that receives on a channel it is handed;
  `reject_channel_receive_held_expr` for one reached through an arrow whose
  expression body calls it). A function that
  receives only on a channel of its own opens a scope to fill it, which R5
  refuses under a lock already.

**What a channel program means.** The receiver sees every value sent, each
sender's in its send order. How two senders' values interleave is the
scheduler's natively and spawn order under Node, so a receiver whose answer
depends on it — not a count or an integer sum, but the first value, or an
`f64` sum whose partial sums are not exact — is its author's obligation, as
for the lock. A task's channel is checked where it can be read, at the
`spawn`; a parallel body has no way to reach one, because a task calls no
`parallelMapInto` and a channel is made only beside a scope. `select` stays
declined (wp29 §9).

<a id="what-nish---fix-writes-for-a-thread-program" style="scroll-margin-top: 65px"></a>

## What `nish --fix` writes for a thread program

The thread refusals end with the code to write instead (each pinned whole by
its `tests/wordings` case), and six of them carry a fix that `nish --fix` applies, each only where the source alone decides the
replacement (`tests/fix/thread-*`; the refused shapes are its `thread-nofix-*`
cases):

| Refusal | The fix | Left alone |
| --- | --- | --- |
| NL2388, a `scope()` not bound by `using` | `const s = scope()` becomes `using s = scope()` | a `let`, which is assigned again |
| NL2465, a `lock()` not bound by `using` | `const g = m.lock()` becomes `using g = m.lock()` | a `let` |
| NL2511, a `spawn` with no destination, whose task answers a number or a `boolean` | `const answer = new Array<T>(1)` above the scope's `using`, and `, answer, 0` after the arguments | a `spawn` in a loop, where every task would write one slot; an answer that is not a number or a `boolean` |
| NL2506, a task's arrow that captures a `let` | `const kNow = k` just before the statement, and the arrow reads `kNow`: the value it would have read when it ran | a `let` another argument names; a `let` a `for` header declares, where no statement before the call is in the loop |
| NL2500, the same in a `parallelMap` | the same | the same |
| NL2484, an arrow that uses a `Channel` | the arrow moves to a `const` above the top-level statement it is written in, named for the function and `Task` (`mainTask`), and the call names it | an arrow that captures, or leaves a parameter's or its result's type out, which would not check at the top level |

## Shared memory between processes: `nish/sync/shm` and `nish/sync/ring`

Threads share an address space; processes share nothing unless they map the
same memory. `nish/sync/shm` maps a **named region** that every process of
the same user can open, and `nish/sync/ring` builds lock-free queues of byte
records in one, so prefork workers can hand work to an owner process without a
socket:

```typescript
import { ACQ_REL, ACQUIRE, createRegion, unlinkRegion } from "nish/sync/shm";
import { initSpscRing, spscRingBytes } from "nish/sync/ring";

export const main = (): i32 => {
  const region = createRegion("lang-demo", 64 + spscRingBytes(4096)).expect("create");
  region.addI64(0, toI64(1), ACQ_REL); // a counter every process may bump
  const ring = initSpscRing(region, 64, 4096, true); // a ring after it
  const job: u8[] = [1, 2, 3];
  ring.tryPush(job, 0, job.length); // false when full
  const got: u8[] = new Array<u8>(16);
  const n: i32 = ring.tryPop(got, 0); // 3, or RING_EMPTY
  console.log(`${region.loadI64(0, ACQUIRE)} ${n}`);
  unlinkRegion("lang-demo").expect("unlink");
  return 0;
};
```

- **A region is named, never inherited.** A Nish program has no `fork`, and
  every descriptor is close-on-exec, so an anonymous mapping or a `memfd`
  cannot reach a child; a name can. `createRegion(name, bytes)` makes one,
  zeroed, mode 0600, and refuses a name that exists (`SHM_EXISTS`), so a name
  another user planted is never adopted. `openRegion(name)` maps one this
  user made, and refuses one owned by someone else, open to group or others,
  reached through a symbolic link, or (on Linux) not a regular file or with a
  second hard link (`SHM_ACCESS`). A name is 1 to 30 of `A-Z a-z 0-9 . _ -`,
  not starting with `.`; a size is 1 byte to 1 GiB. Errors are a `Result`
  with the errno (`SHM_NOT_FOUND`, `SHM_INVALID`, `SHM_TOO_MANY`, ...).
- **Lifetime.** The name lasts until `unlinkRegion`, even past every process
  that mapped it, which is how a process started later finds it. A mapping
  lasts until `close()` or the process's exit, when the kernel unmaps it. A
  thread may hold 63 regions at once.
- **Every access is checked, as an array index is.** `loadI32`, `storeI32`,
  `addI32`, `exchangeI32`, `compareExchangeI32` and their `I64` twins take an
  `i32` byte offset; a slot must lie wholly inside the region and at a multiple
  of its width, or the access panics naming the offset (`nish/sync/shm: slot
  offset 4 is not a multiple of 8, the slot's width`). `read` and `write` copy
  a byte window, checked against both the region and the buffer. No offset
  reaches outside the mapping, whatever a peer wrote into it.
- **Windows: a `u8[]` that is the region's bytes.** `region.lend(at, len)`
  answers a `u8[]` of length `len` whose data is bytes `[at, at + len)` of the
  mapping, checked as `read`'s window is (`nish/sync/shm: byte window at 60 is
  outside the region of 64 bytes`). An index store, `copyBytes` into it or
  `netRead` into it writes the region itself, and every process mapping it
  sees the bytes, with no copy. The window is not atomic: order it with a slot
  (`storeI32(.., RELEASE)` after the bytes, `loadI32(.., ACQUIRE)` before
  reading them), as a ring does. `region.giveBack(window)` answers its length
  and empties it, and `close()` empties every window the region lent, so an
  index after either is `index out of range: 0 >= 0`, never a read of an
  unmapped page. A `pop` or a shorter `length` keeps a window; a **push past
  its length moves it** off the region into the program's memory, as any push
  past capacity does, and `giveBack` then panics (`window of length 17 is no
  longer the region's bytes: a push moved it`), as it does for a window
  given back twice or lent by another region.
- **The reuse rule.** Each `lend` without `reuse` takes a header of 48 bytes
  that lasts until the process exits, since the program may hold the array
  past any `giveBack` or `close`. A loop that lends again passes the window it
  gave back, `region.lend(at, len, window)`, which re-points that header and
  takes no memory; a `reuse` that is still lent, or not this region's, panics.
  Windows belong to the thread that lent them, as the region does.
- **Why an intrinsic, not FFI.** `lend` and `giveBack` are the module's two
  compiler-known functions (`src/shm-window.ts`), whose bodies the compiler
  writes as a call of `nishshm_lend` / `nishshm_give_back`: a foreign function
  may take a `u8[]` but answers no array, and a window must be one the program
  indexes. Known by its package and path, as `nish:region` is, the call is
  marked as writing through and keeping its array and as possibly changing
  any array's length, so no length the bounds proof knew survives it, and a
  region's `close()` is marked the same way.
- **Orderings are C11's**: `RELAXED`, `ACQUIRE`, `RELEASE`, `ACQ_REL`,
  `SEQ_CST`, plus `fence(order)`. Each access is one LLVM `load atomic`,
  `store atomic`, `atomicrmw` or `cmpxchg` with that ordering; an ordering an
  access cannot take (a load with `RELEASE`) panics. A compare-exchange
  answers the value it found, so it succeeded when that equals `expected`.
- **Waking.** `waitI32(at, expected, timeoutMs)` sleeps while the slot holds
  `expected` and `wake(at, count)` wakes sleepers, in any process: Linux's
  shared futex. Darwin and wasi answer `SHM_UNSUPPORTED` (-95) from both, and
  a program there polls.
- **Rings.** `SpscRing` (one producer, one consumer, records of any length
  up to its capacity) and `MpscRing` (any number of producers, fixed slots)
  live at a 64-byte-aligned `base` in a region: `initSpscRing` /
  `initMpscRing` write the header once, `attachSpscRing` / `attachMpscRing`
  read it in another process. `tryPush` answers `false` when full; `tryPop`
  answers the record's length, `RING_EMPTY` or `RING_TOO_SMALL`; `popBatch`
  takes every record ready. A ring made with the doorbell lets `popWait`
  sleep, and a push rings it only when the consumer is asleep, so a busy ring
  makes no system call. Two consumers, or two producers on an `SpscRing`, lose
  or repeat records but never leave the region; a length no record can have
  panics as `the ring is corrupt`.
- **What a program reaches.** The modules call C, so a program that imports
  them reaches [`ffi`](builtins.md#capabilities) (and `clock`, for `popWait`'s deadline)
  and `--deny ffi` refuses it; under `--sandbox` a region, being a file in
  `/dev/shm`, needs `fs.read` and `fs.write` as well. They are native only:
  `--emit-ts` refuses them, since Node's `SharedArrayBuffer` is shared between
  threads of one process, not between processes. A region belongs to the
  thread that mapped it. A program that imports neither module is unchanged.
  Tested by `tests/link/sync_shm`, `tests/link/sync_shm_window`,
  `tests/link/sync_ring` and `tests/link/sync_shm_deny_ffi`; the design, its measurements and the threads
  it was weighed against are `docs/wp47-shared-memory.md`, and the threat model
  is [`docs/security/shm.md`](../../security/shm.md).

## Random numbers: `Rng` in `nish/random`

`new Rng(seed)` is a generator of pseudo-random numbers whose every answer
depends on its `i32` seed alone, and is the same natively and under Node:

```typescript
import { Rng } from "nish/random";

export const main = (): i32 => {
  const r = new Rng(42);
  const die: i32 = r.nextInt(1, 6); // 1 to 6, each with equal chance
  const u: f64 = r.nextF64(); // in [0, 1)
  console.log(`${die} ${u < 1.0}`);
  return 0;
};
```

- **`nextI32()`** answers the next 32 bits as an `i32`, and **`nextF64()`** a
  double in [0, 1) built from 53 bits of two steps. The state walks a Weyl
  sequence (an odd increment, wrapping) through all 2^32 values, and each
  answer is MurmurHash3's 32-bit finaliser of it, so every seed, 0 included,
  starts a full sequence, and seeds 1, 2 and 3 start unrelated ones. It is not
  for cryptography: a key comes from `crypto.getRandomValues`.
- **`nextInt(lo, hi)`** answers an `i32` in [lo, hi], both ends included, each
  with equal chance. It refuses the few `nextI32()` draws below 2^32 mod the
  span and answers `lo` plus the draw mod the span, so no answer is likelier
  than another; fewer than half the draws are refused, so a call takes under
  two steps on average. `nextInt(-2147483648, 2147483647)` is one `nextI32()`,
  and `lo > hi` panics with `Rng.nextInt: lo is greater than hi`.
- **The same bits under Node** are the point of the design. The
  operations that wrap are `wrappingAdd`, `wrappingSub` and `wrappingMul` from
  [`nish:unsafe`](builtins.md#nishunsafe-unchecked-access-and-defined-wrapping), every shift has a constant count,
  `nextInt` reads its unsigned counts through `i32` compares and remainders of
  non-negative values, and `nextF64`'s double is exact, so `tests/link/std_random` prints the same lines
  both ways.
- **A parallel body or a task steps an `Rng` it made itself**, which is its
  own memory (`const r = new Rng(i)`, "Nor is a write into an object's own
  slots" under [data parallelism](#data-parallelism-nishthreads)); a
  generator shared by several tasks would be a shared write, and is refused as
  one. Seed each task's own from its index.

## Byte search: `indexOfAny` in `nish/text`

`indexOfAny(text, bytes, from)` answers the first index at or after `from`
whose byte is one of `bytes`, or -1 ([wp38-simd.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp38-simd.md) §3.1). It is
the scan a parser spends its time in — the next `"` or `\` in a JSON string,
the next delimiter in a line — and natively it reads 16 or 32 bytes at a time.

```typescript
import { indexOfAny } from "nish/text";

export const main = (): i32 => {
  const line = "key: \"value\", next";
  console.log(`${indexOfAny(line, "\":", 0)}`);   // 3, the colon
  console.log(`${indexOfAny(line, ",", 99)}`);    // -1: `from` is clamped to the length
  return 0;
};
```

- **The set is 1 to 16 ASCII bytes, or the call panics.** An empty set
  (`indexOfAny: the set must hold 1 to 16 bytes`) matches nothing and is a
  mistake rather than a search; seventeen bytes is more than one vector of the
  kernel compares; and a byte of 128 or more
  (`indexOfAny: every byte of the set must be ASCII`) would be one byte of a
  multi-byte sequence natively and a UTF-16 unit under Node, which find
  different things (`tests/link/std_text_index_of_any_empty_set`,
  `_long_set`, `_non_ascii_set`).
- **`from` is clamped to `[0, text.length]`**, as `substring` clamps: a
  negative `from` searches from the start, and one at or past the length
  answers -1. The answer is a byte offset, like `s.length`; an ASCII byte
  never occurs inside a multi-byte UTF-8 sequence, so a non-ASCII `text` is
  searched as it is and only its ASCII bytes match. Under Node the offset is a
  UTF-16 one, so the two agree on what was found and, once a non-ASCII
  character precedes it, not on where (`tests/link/std_text_index_of_any`).
- **The module is ordinary Nish, and the walker is the meaning.**
  `std/text.ts` writes `indexOfAny` as its checks and its clamp followed by
  one call to a private walker, a loop over `charCodeAt`, which is what runs
  under Node. The compiler recognises that call by module and name
  (`src/kernels.ts`) and emits the runtime's `nish_str_index_of_any` in its
  place; everything around it is emitted as written, so the kernel is only
  ever handed a clamped `from` and a set of 1 to 16 bytes. The package is part
  of the test: a root-package file that happens to sit at `std/text.ts` is an
  ordinary module, and its walker is called as written. The kernel picks a
  scalar, a 16-byte (SSE2 or NEON) or a 32-byte (AVX2) path on its first call,
  and `NISH_SIMD=scalar|base|avx2` pins it.
- **It is variable-time.** How long the search takes says where the first
  match is, so it is never for secret data: `std/crypto` does not call it on
  one, and `nish:secret`'s `expose` lets it through only because it touches
  nothing outside its two strings.

On a 1 MiB text with a match every 4,099 bytes, the kernel scans at 14 GB/s
with AVX2 and 7 GB/s on the 16-byte path, against 1.6 GB/s for the same
walker compiled as written (`bench/index-of-any.ts`).

## Fixed digits and a split limit: `toFixed` and `splitLimit` in `nish/text`

Nish has no methods on a number and no optional parameters, so JavaScript's
`x.toFixed(n)` and `text.split(sep, limit)` are two functions of `nish/text`.
Each is the method it stands for, read as TypeScript: under Node the module
runs as written and answers what the method answers, and natively it answers
the same bytes (`tests/link/std_text_to_fixed`, `tests/link/std_text_split_limit`,
whose every line `tests/run.js` also holds to Node's own method).

```typescript
import { splitLimit, toFixed } from "nish/text";

export const main = (): i32 => {
  console.log(toFixed(1.005, 2));                     // 1.00: 1.005 is stored a little below
  console.log(toFixed(2.5, 0));                       // 3: a tie goes away from zero
  console.log(splitLimit("a,b,c", ",", 2).join("|")); // a|b: the rest is dropped
  return 0;
};
```

- **`toFixed(x, digits)` rounds the exact binary value**, as ECMA-262 does:
  `1.005` is stored as 1.00499999999999989…, so it gives `"1.00"`, while
  `8.345` is stored a little above and gives `"8.35"`; an exact tie rounds
  away from zero, so `toFixed(-2.5, 0)` is `"-3"`. `digits` is 0 to 100, and
  any other count panics (`toFixed: digits must be 0 to 100`) where JavaScript
  throws a `RangeError`. `NaN`, the infinities and any `x` of magnitude 1e21 or
  more answer `${x}`, as JavaScript does; `-0` gives `"0.00"`, and a negative
  `x` that rounds to zero keeps its sign (`toFixed(-0.0001, 2)` is `"-0.00"`).
  It is written in Nish over an array of decimal digits, so it is exact for
  every `f64`, the subnormals included, and it needs no runtime C.
- **`splitLimit(text, sep, limit)` keeps the first `limit` pieces** of
  `split(text, sep)` and drops the rest, rather than joining them into the
  last; a limit of 0 gives `[]`. A negative limit keeps every piece, because
  JavaScript reads the limit through `ToUint32` and -1 becomes 4294967295;
  that makes `splitLimit(text, sep, -1)` the same as `split(text, sep)`. An
  empty separator panics (`splitLimit: an empty separator`) whatever the
  limit, as `split`'s does, even where JavaScript would answer `[]`.

## Byte runs: `skipBlank`, `skipDigits`, `skipJsonText`, `skipJsonPlain` and `copyBytes` in `nish/bytes`

The four runs answer the first index in `[from, to)` of a `u8[]` whose byte
is not in their class, or `to` when every byte there is; `copyBytes` copies a
window of one array into another, or into itself
([wp38-simd.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp38-simd.md), S6a). They are the scans and the copy a parser
spends its time in, and `std/json` is written over them.

```typescript
import { copyBytes, skipBlank, skipDigits, skipJsonPlain, skipJsonText } from "nish/bytes";

export const main = (): i32 => {
  const text: u8[] = [32, 10, 52, 50, 44, 34, 104, 105, 34]; // " \n42,\"hi\""
  const start = skipBlank(text, 0, 9);
  console.log(`${start} ${skipDigits(text, start, 9)}`);   // 2 4
  console.log(`${skipJsonText(text, 6, 9)}`);              // 8, the closing quote
  console.log(`${skipJsonPlain(text, 0, 9)}`);             // 1, the newline
  const word: u8[] = [0, 0];
  copyBytes(word, 0, text, 6, 2);
  console.log(`${word[0]} ${word[1]}`);                    // 104 105
  return 0;
};
```

- **The classes.** `skipBlank` skips JSON's four blanks (space, tab, newline,
  carriage return) and `skipDigits` the ASCII digits. `skipJsonText` skips
  what a JSON string holds as itself: printable ASCII other than `"` and `\`
  (DEL included, which JSON does not escape), and every well-formed UTF-8
  sequence (RFC 3629 §4) that ends before `to`. It stops at a quote, a
  backslash or a control byte, and at the lead byte of a sequence that is
  overlong, a surrogate, past U+10FFFF, a stray continuation byte or cut short
  by `to`, so where it stops is the byte a decoder has to look at.
  `skipJsonPlain` skips what a JSON writer copies without an escape: every
  byte from 0x20 up other than `"` and `\`, DEL and 0x80–0xff included, with
  no UTF-8 check. It stops at a quote, a backslash or a byte below 0x20.
- **The runs never panic.** `to` is clamped into `[0, b.length]` and `from`
  into `[0, to]`, as `indexOfAny` clamps: a negative `from` scans from the
  start, and a `from` at or past `to` answers it
  (`tests/link/std_bytes_runs`).
- **`copyBytes` panics on a range outside its array.** A negative `count`, or
  a window that does not lie inside `src` or `dst`, panics
  `copyBytes: the range lies outside an array` before any byte is written
  (`tests/link/std_bytes_copy_outside`). Overlapping ranges of one array copy
  as if every byte were read before any was written, as `copyWithin` does.
- **The walkers are the meaning.** Each public function clamps or checks its
  range, then makes one call to a private walker, a plain loop over the bytes,
  which is what runs under Node. Natively the compiler recognises that call by
  module and name (`src/kernels.ts`), as it does `indexOfAny`'s, and emits the
  runtime's `nish_bytes_skip_blank`, `nish_bytes_skip_digits` or
  `nish_bytes_skip_json_text` or `nish_bytes_skip_json_plain` (`runtime/runtime-bytes.c`) in its place, or one
  `llvm.memmove` for the copy. The kernels pick a scalar, a 16-byte (SSE2,
  NEON or wasm SIMD) or a 32-byte (AVX2) path on their first call, and
  `NISH_SIMD=scalar|base|avx2` pins it, except in a freestanding wasm32 build,
  which has no environment to read it from.
- **The runs are variable-time.** How long one takes says how long the run is,
  so they are for text, never for secret data: `std/crypto` does not call
  them.

## SQLite: `nish/sqlite`

`nish/sqlite` is the SQLite C library, linked into a program that imports the
module, with a `Database` and a `Statement` to drive it. A statement is
prepared once and bound, stepped and reset as often as wanted:

```typescript
import { openDatabase, OPEN_READWRITE, OPEN_CREATE } from "nish/sqlite";

export const main = (): i32 => {
  const db = openDatabase(":memory:", OPEN_READWRITE | OPEN_CREATE).expect("open");
  db.exec("CREATE TABLE t (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT)").expect("create");
  const insert = db.prepare("INSERT INTO t (name) VALUES (?1)").expect("prepare");
  insert.bindText(1, "ada").expect("bind");
  insert.step().expect("insert");
  insert.reset().expect("reset");
  console.log(`${db.lastInsertRowid()}`);
  db.close().expect("close");
  return 0;
};
```

- **Every failure is a `Result`.** `openDatabase` and `prepare` answer a
  `SqliteError`, with SQLite's extended code (`extendedCode`, such as 2067 for
  `SQLITE_CONSTRAINT_UNIQUE`), its primary code (`code`, the low byte) and
  SQLite's message. Every other call answers the bare extended code, and
  `error(code)` on the `Database` or `Statement` that answered it builds the
  `SqliteError`, so a failure allocates only for the caller who asks.
  `step()` answers `true` with a row to read and `false` when the statement
  has finished.
- **A row allocates nothing.** Binding, `step`, `reset`, `columnI64`,
  `columnF64` and `columnInto` answer scalars; `columnInto(c, buf, at)` copies
  a text or blob column into the caller's `u8[]`, and answers its length,
  copying only when all of it fits. `columnText(c)` is the call that makes a
  string, and it stops at the first NUL byte. Parameters count from 1 and columns from 0, as in SQLite.
- **`exec(sql)`** runs every statement of `sql` and discards any rows, and
  `begin()`, `commit()` and `rollback()` are `exec` of `BEGIN`, `COMMIT` and
  `ROLLBACK`; pragmas, such as `journal_mode=WAL`, are SQL too. A binding is
  copied by SQLite, and `reset` keeps the bindings.
- **A handle is an `i32`** into tables the C adapter keeps per thread. `close`
  finalizes every statement the connection still has, and a handle used after
  `close` or `finalize` answers `SQLITE_MISUSE` rather than reaching freed
  memory. A connection and its statements belong to the thread that opened
  them.
- **It reaches `ffi`.** The module calls C through `declare function`, so a
  program that imports it is reported with [`ffi`](builtins.md#capabilities) and
  `--deny ffi` refuses it, naming the call. The files SQLite opens are opened
  by C, which the `fs.read` and `fs.write` capabilities do not see. It is
  tested natively and under `--profile wasi` (`tests/link/std_sqlite*`).

## Interfaces and object literals

```ts
interface Pair { first: number; second: number; }

const swap = (p: Pair): Pair => ({ first: p.second, second: p.first });
```

- An interface is a struct type with the same layout rules as a class, with
  fields only: a method, or an accessor signature `get x(): i32`, is
  `` Interface `Shape` cannot declare methods (interfaces describe layout only) ``
  (`tests/cases/reject_iface_method`, `reject_iface_accessor`; a field may
  still be called `get` or `set`), `extends`
  is ``Interface inheritance (`extends`) is not supported; list every field``
  (`tests/cases/reject_iface_extends`, `reject_generic_interface_extends`),
  an index signature is
  `` Index signatures are not supported in interface `Point` (object layout is fixed) ``
  (`reject_iface_index_signature`), a construct or call signature,
  `new (): Point` or `(x: i32): i32`, is
  `` Unsupported interface member in `Point`: ConstructSignature `` (or
  `CallSignature`, `reject_iface_member_unsupported`), `declare interface` is
  `` `declare interface` is not supported ``, and `new` on an
  interface is `` Cannot `new` interface `Pair` `` (`tests/cases/reject_cls_new_interface`).
- An **object literal** allocates in the arena and stores every property in
  source order. It must set every field exactly once (`` is missing field `second` ``,
  `tests/cases/reject_cls_literal_missing`; `` `Pair` has no field `third` ``,
  `reject_cls_literal_extra`), with plain identifier keys and `key: value`
  or shorthand members: a key written as a string or a number is
  `Object literal keys must be plain identifiers` (`reject_cls_literal_key`),
  and a method or an accessor is
  ``Unsupported object literal member: MethodDeclaration (only `key: value`)``
  (`GetAccessor`, `SetAccessor`; `reject_cls_literal_member`) — `get`, `set`
  and `async` stay keys and shorthands (`{ get: 1 }`, `{ get }`). It takes its type from the context: a variable
  annotation, the enclosing function's return type, the parameter it is
  passed to, the field or variable it is assigned to, or the field of an
  enclosing literal; otherwise
  `Object literal needs a contextual class or interface type`
  (`tests/cases/reject_cls_literal_no_context`, `cls_interface_literal`,
  `cls_nested`). That context reaches a *nested* object literal and a `null`,
  and stops there: a numeric literal written for a field keeps the mode's
  default type (see "Numeric literals"), and `[]` has no element type at all
  in this position — `{ xs: [] }` is `Empty array literal needs a type
  annotation` and wants a named array instead
  (`tests/cases/reject_struct_field_empty_array`). A value of the wrong type
  is `` Field `code` of `IoError` expects a value of type i32, got f64 ``
  (`reject_struct_field_f64`).
- A **nullable context** gives an object literal the struct inside it:
  wherever one of the contexts above expects `E | null` — a declared local,
  a `return`, an arrow's concise body, a ternary arm whose other arm is
  `null`, a parameter, or a field — the literal is an `E`, checked against
  `E`'s fields as above, and that `E` converts to `E | null` as any other
  `E` value does, the same pointer with no wrapper
  (`tests/cases/obj_lit_nullable_ternary`, `obj_lit_nullable_return`,
  `obj_lit_nullable_arrow`, `obj_lit_nullable_local`,
  `obj_lit_nullable_field`; `reject_obj_lit_nullable_field`). A ternary
  with no declared type around it gives neither arm a struct, so
  `const z = c ? { v: 7 } : null` is still
  `Object literal needs a contextual class or interface type`
  (`reject_obj_lit_nullable_context`).
- A **class with methods** is made only by `new`. Natively a literal would
  take the class's layout and its methods, but under Node it is a plain
  object, and a call on it throws, so wherever a context above types a
  literal as such a class it is
  `` `Counter` has methods, so it is made only by `new`: an object literal would be a plain object under Node, with none of the methods the class is used through. Write `new Counter(...)` ``
  (NL2556; `tests/cases/reject_class_literal_decl`, `…_return`,
  `…_arrow_body`, `…_call_arg`, `…_method_arg`, `…_new_arg`,
  `…_array_elem`, `…_push`, `…_index_assign`, `…_map_set`,
  `…_record_field`, `…_assign`, `…_field_assign`, `…_ternary`, `…_paren`, `…_alias`,
  `…_coalesce`, `…_coalesce_chain`, `…_coalesce_field`, `…_coalesce_call`,
  `…_coalesce_map`, `…_coalesce_optional`, `…_coalesce_ternary`,
  `…_equality`, `…_index_of`, `…_math_max`, `…_fn_param`, `…_unary`,
  `…_compound_bitwise`, `…_compound_arith`, `…_nullable`, `…_generic_class`, `…_generic_target`, `…_generic_method`,
  `…_imported`). A generic method counts as a method; a constructor does
  not. A class with fields alone, and an interface, still take a literal
  (`tests/cases/cls_literal_methodless`). The `nish/threads` classes keep
  their own refusal, NL2515 (see "Atomics"), and a class holding a `Secret`
  keeps NL2545.
- An **object spread** `{ ...s, x: 1 }` copies `s`'s fields into the
  literal, one store per field, and is otherwise the literal written out:
  the spread and `{ x: 1, y: s.y }` emit the same IR, an `alloca` where the
  literal stays local and an arena allocation where it escapes
  (`tests/run.js` "object spread", `tests/cases/obj_spread_twin`). Each
  spread is evaluated once, in source order with the entries around it, and
  the entry written later wins: a field set after a spread overrides it, and
  of two spreads the later one supplies the fields both have; only the
  fields no later entry overrides are stored
  (`tests/cases/obj_spread_order`). A field holding an object is copied as
  the reference it is (`obj_spread_nested`), a class instance spreads its
  fields and none of its methods, as Node's spread does
  (`obj_spread_class`), and a nullable source spreads once narrowed
  (`obj_spread_narrowed`); a write to the source after the spread leaves the
  copy as it was (`obj_spread_class`). The literal must still set every
  field of its type, by the spread or by name: a spread that supplies only
  some of them leaves the rest
  `` Object literal for `Point` is missing field `z` ``
  (`reject_object_spread_missing_field`). Each form whose Node reading would
  differ from the copy is refused:

  | Form | Code | Tests |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | no contextual class or interface type, `const o = { ...s }`: ``An object literal with a spread needs a contextual class or interface type, whose layout the spread's fields are copied into: annotate the variable (`const p: P = { ...s, x: 1 }`)`` | NL2709 | `reject_object_spread_no_target`, `reject_ffi_handle_walk_spread` |
  | a source that is not a class or interface value, `{ ...n }` for an `i32` | NL2705 | `reject_object_spread` |
  | a source that may be `null`, which Node spreads as no field at all: narrow it first | NL2703 | `reject_object_spread_nullable` |
  | a union source, whose fields depend on the variant it holds | NL2704 | `reject_object_spread_union` |
  | a class instance with a field the target does not declare, which Node would carry on the object | NL2706 | `reject_object_spread_class_extra` |
  | an interface value with a field the target does not declare | NL2707 | `reject_object_spread_extra_field` |
  | a copied field whose type differs from the target's, `i32` into `i64`: the copy converts nothing. A field a later entry sets by name is not copied, so its type is not checked (`obj_spread_override_type`); one a later spread supplies is still checked | NL2708 | `reject_object_spread_field_type` |
  | a field set by name before a spread that always overwrites it, TypeScript's TS2783 | NL2710 | `reject_object_spread_overwritten` |

  An interface value may hold any class that implements it, and such a
  class may declare fields after the interface's prefix (see `implements`
  below): Node copies every own field of the instance, the native copy only
  the interface's. So once the whole program is checked, a spread of an
  interface `I` into a type that lacks a field of some class implementing
  `I` is
  `` Spread of `Named` into `Tagged` may spread an instance of `Item`, which implements it with field `weight` besides: … ``
  (NL3055, `reject_object_spread_width`); spread a value of the class type
  instead. A spread into the typed JSON options of a class is NL2711
  (`reject_json_options_spread`). One gap remains: Nish accepts `private`
  on a field and ignores it, so a class instance with a `private` field
  spreads into a type that declares that field, where `tsc` refuses the
  spread; under Node the copy is the same object either way. A computed key is still refused
  (NL1041). NL1061, Phase 0's old refusal of every object spread, is
  retired and never reused.
- `readonly` on an interface field forbids every assignment (`i.a = 2` is
  `` Cannot assign to readonly field `a` of `Config` ``,
  `tests/cases/reject_cls_readonly_interface`); literals still set it. The
  message drops the class form's "outside its constructor", because an
  interface has none to point at.
- **`class C implements I`** requires `I`'s fields to be `C`'s **first**
  fields, in the same order and with identical types; `C` may declare more
  after them (`tests/cases/cls_implements_prefix`). A missing one is
  `` does not implement `Point3`: it lacks field `z: i32` ``
  (`reject_cls_implements_short`) and a mismatched one is
  `` field 1 is `width: i32` in `Shape` but `height: i32` in `Square` ``
  (`reject_cls_implements_mismatch`); both end
  `(the interface's fields must be the class's first fields, in order)`.

  A `C` then converts to `I` wherever an `I` is expected (initializer,
  return, argument, assignment, field store, ternary arm, `I[]` element) by
  one `bitcast`, because the two address the same bytes at the same offsets
  for every field `I` names; a class with the right fields that does not
  list `I` is not assignable (`tests/cases/cls_implements`,
  `reject_cls_not_implements`). Nothing converts back: there is no downcast,
  no `as`, no `instanceof`. The class's own fields after the prefix reuse
  its tail padding, exactly as clang lays out the same C struct
  (`tests/layout/structs.ts`, classes `K`, `L`, `M`).

  **This is the only widening in the language.** Since WP25 a class is a
  prefix of nothing but the interfaces it names, which is what lets two
  classes with different tails be held in one `I[]` and operated on by one
  function (`tests/cases/cls_implements_prefix`,
  `tests/differential/corpus/class_prefix`) — the job `extends` used to do,
  without a dispatch rule to get wrong.

## Calling C

**`declare function name(params): T;` declares a C function this program calls
but does not define.** The symbol is the identifier — no mangling, no prefix —
and the call is an ordinary call:

```ts
declare function abs(n: i32): i32;
```

```llvm
declare i32 @abs(i32)
  %0 = call i32 @abs(i32 %n)
```

The spelling is TypeScript's own ambient declaration, and `declare` is a
*contextual* keyword: a variable may still be called `declare`.

**A parameter is a scalar, a `CPtr`, a borrowed `string`, a `u8[]` buffer
with its count or a borrowed `declare class`; a return is a scalar, a `CPtr` or
a copied `string`** — `i32`,
`i64`, `u8`, `u16`, `u32`, `u64`, `f32`, `f64`, `boolean`, `void`, the foreign
pointer below, `string` and `string | null` in either position, and
[a buffer](#a-u8-parameter-a-buffer-and-its-count) and
[a C struct](#a-declare-class-a-c-struct-lent-by-pointer) as a parameter. Any
other class or an interface is rejected with
`` and a declared C function takes scalars, `CPtr`, a `string` it borrows as
`const char *` and a `u8[]` buffer followed by its `u64` count, or a `declare
class` it borrows by pointer `` in a
parameter (`reject_ffi_class_param`), any other array with
`` the only array a declared C function takes is a `u8[]` or a `readonly u8[]` ``
(`tests/cases/reject_ffi_string_array_param`: a `string[]` too, which would be
a `char **` the compiler built per call) and
`` returns a scalar, a `CPtr` or a `string` it copies from a `const char *` ``
in the return position (`reject_ffi_string_array_return`). This is
not a stylistic limit: **the only pointer this compiler allocated that crosses
the boundary is a string C reads for the length of the call, and the only one
C hands back that the program keeps is a copy it made**, so there is nothing for
a foreign function to capture or free, which is what lets the escape analysis
stay correct without knowing anything about the callee.

### A `string` parameter: borrowed for the length of the call

**A `string` parameter is C's NUL-terminated `const char *`, and C borrows it:
a foreign function may read the bytes until it returns and may not keep the
address.** A function that keeps its argument — `putenv`, `setvbuf`'s buffer, a
callback's context — is declared to take a `CPtr` instead, and the program hands
it a copy C made (`tests/cases/ffi_string_param`, `ffi_string_param_arena`,
[cookbook](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/IR_COOKBOOK.md#a-string-parameter-borrowed-as-const-char-)):

```ts
declare function strdup(s: string): CPtr | null;
declare function putenv(entry: CPtr): i32; // keeps the pointer: C's, not ours

const kept = strdup("MODE=fast");
if (kept !== null) {
  putenv(kept);
}
```

```llvm
declare i8* @strdup(i8*)
  %0 = getelementptr inbounds i8, i8* bitcast ({ i64, [10 x i8] }* @.str.0 to i8*), i64 8
  %1 = call i8* @strdup(i8* %0)
```

- **The argument is the string's own bytes, with no copy.** A `nish_str` stores
  them NUL-terminated, a literal included, so the call passes the address eight
  bytes into it. The escape analysis treats the argument as a read, the way it
  treats a string `console.log` prints: an arena scope that holds it is released
  after the call returns, and the call is never a `tail` call.
- **C may not write through it.** A literal lives in read-only constant data and
  an arena string is shared freely, so a C function that writes into its
  argument (`strtok`, `mkstemp`) corrupts a value the program still holds, or
  faults. Such a function takes a `CPtr` buffer allocated through C. The
  compiler cannot check this rule; it is the declaration's author's word, like
  the borrow.
- **A string that holds a NUL byte panics before the call**, because C would
  read the NUL as the end of the string — `"secret\0.txt"` would pass a
  `.txt` check in the program and name `secret` in C. The message names the
  callee, the argument's position and the parameter:
  `` `strlen`: argument 1 (s) holds a NUL byte, which C would read as the end of
  the string `` (`tests/cases/panics_ffi_nul`). That is the
  [`ffi-nul` panic site](semantics-decisions.md#panic-sites). A literal with no NUL in it is proved
  at compile time, so `puts("hello")` has no check and no site; every other
  string is checked with one scan of the bytes C is about to read anyway.
- **`string | null` passes `NULL` for `null`**, and checks only a string.
- **The declaration carries no attribute** for a string parameter: `nocapture`
  and `readonly` would restate the borrow as an LLVM fact the C body need not
  honour, which would be a miscompile rather than a broken contract.

<a id="a-string-result-copied-out-of-cs-const-char-" style="scroll-margin-top: 65px"></a>

### A `string` result: copied out of C's `const char *`

**A `declare function` that returns `string` or `string | null` answers C's
NUL-terminated `const char *`, and the program copies its bytes into the arena
at the call.** C keeps its buffer — `strerror`'s table, `getenv`'s environment,
`setlocale`'s static, which the next call may overwrite — and the copy is the
program's own string from then on, placed, kept and released like any other
allocation of the function that made the call (`tests/cases/ffi_string_return`,
[cookbook](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/IR_COOKBOOK.md#a-string-result-copied-out-of-const-char-)):

```ts
declare function strerror(errnum: i32): string;
declare function getenv(name: string): string | null;

console.log(strerror(2)); // No such file or directory
const home = getenv("HOME");
```

```llvm
  %0 = call i8* @strerror(i32 2)
  %1 = icmp eq i8* %0, null
  br i1 %1, label %ffi.null, label %ffi.copy

ffi.copy:
  %2 = call i8* @nish.ffi.str(i8* %0)
```

- **The copy is one scan for the NUL and one `nish_str_new`**, in a private
  helper the module defines once (`@nish.ffi.str`). C's pointer is never held
  past it, so a buffer C reuses or frees later cannot reach the program.
- **Every call's copy is new, and is the calling function's allocation**, as
  `s.substring(...)` is: a loop that keeps one keeps it past the pass, and a
  `using a = arena()` block that would release one held outside it is refused,
  as it is for any fresh string (`tests/cases/ffi_string_loops`,
  `reject_ffi_string_arena`).
- **The copy follows the call, so a call with a `string` result is never a
  `tail` call**: a C function that answers a pointer into its argument
  (`strchr`, `strstr`) is read before that argument's arena scope is released.
- **`string | null` reads `NULL` as `null`**, tested before the copy but with
  no panic site.
- **A `string` result that is `NULL` panics after the call**, because a
  `string` cannot hold it: `` `getenv` returned NULL for a `string` result;
  declare it `string | null` `` (`tests/cases/panics_ffi_null`). That is the
  [`ffi-null` panic site](semantics-decisions.md#panic-sites). Declare the result `string | null`
  whenever the C function's manual says it may answer `NULL`.
- **A result C allocated for the caller to free (`strdup`, `realpath` with no
  buffer) is a `CPtr`, not a `string`**: the copy would leave C's allocation
  with no one to free it. Declare it `CPtr | null`, copy it with
  [`readCString`](#readcstring-a-string-out-of-a-buffer-c-owns), and pass the
  pointer back to `free`.

### `CPtr`: the pointer a C function hands back

**`CPtr` is an address C owns.** It is eight bytes and `i8*` in the IR, and that
is the whole of what the compiler knows about it: it is not arena memory, not a
`%struct`, not a `nish_str`, and its lifetime is the C library's business
(`tests/cases/ffi_pointer`, [cookbook](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/IR_COOKBOOK.md#cptr-the-pointer-a-c-function-hands-back)).

```ts
declare function calloc(count: u64, size: u64): CPtr | null;
declare function free(block: CPtr): void;
```

- **It may be written in a `declare function` signature and on a local that
  holds one, and nowhere else.** A field, an array element, a `Result` arm, a
  type argument, and the parameters or return type of a function this program
  defines are all
  `` `CPtr` cannot be ...: a foreign pointer may only appear in a `declare
  function` signature or on a local bound to one ``
  (`reject_ffi_pointer_field`, `reject_ffi_pointer_array`,
  `reject_ffi_pointer_param`, `reject_ffi_pointer_return`,
  `reject_ffi_pointer_type_argument_fn`). The first group
  would put a foreign address inside a value the arena owns and the escape
  analysis walks; the second would put one across a boundary `--emit-header`,
  `--emit-dts` and `--emit-napi` describe, and none of the three has a spelling
  for an address whose provenance and lifetime are unknown. The type-argument
  clause is stated where a generic function or class is instantiated
  (`reject_ffi_pointer_type_argument`), so `new Empty<CPtr>()` is refused even
  when no member of `Empty<T>` names `T`. The fields that may hold a `CPtr`
  are a handle class's and a [`declare class`](#a-declare-class-a-c-struct-lent-by-pointer)'s, below.
- **A `null` reaches C only as the literal.** A `declare function` may return
  `CPtr | null` and may take one, and a call passes a `CPtr | null` parameter
  either the literal `null` — `realpath(path, null)`, `getcwd(null, 0)`, the
