  manual's "pass NULL to have it allocated" — or a pointer narrowed with
  `if (p !== null)`. A nullable pointer the program holds is
  `` Argument 1 of `free` is a `CPtr | null` the program holds: a nullable
  foreign parameter takes the literal `null` or a pointer narrowed with
  `!== null`, so C is never handed a null by a path nobody tested ``
  (NL2539, `reject_ffi_pointer_nullable_variable`), wherever it is held: a
  local, a parenthesised one, a ternary or `??` that may answer it, inside a
  constructor reached by `new` or a method, and through a function parameter
  a `declare function` is passed to (`reject_ffi_pointer_nullable_specialised`).
  So every `NULL` C receives is one the source spells, and a pointer that may
  be `NULL` because C said so is narrowed before it goes back. The narrowing
  is the ordinary nullable one (WP6). The literal lowers to `i8* null`
  (`tests/cases/ffi_owned_string`).
- **No arithmetic, no dereference, no index, no member.** `p + 1` is
  `` Operator `+` requires two operands of the same numeric type ``
  (`reject_ffi_pointer_arithmetic`) and `p[0]` is
  `` Cannot index a value of type CPtr ``. What is left is `=== null`,
  `!== null`, comparing two `CPtr`s, assignment, and passing one to another
  foreign function.
- **It gets no pointer attributes.** `dereferenceable`, `align`, `nonnull`,
  `nocapture` and `readonly` are each a claim about memory this compiler laid
  out, and it laid out none of this; `isPointerParam` in
  `src/attributes.ts` is an allow-list so that a `CPtr` falls out of it
  by construction rather than by a case somebody remembered to write.

### `readCString`: a string out of a buffer C owns

**`readCString(p: CPtr): string`, from
[`nish:unsafe`](builtins.md#nishunsafe-unchecked-access-and-defined-wrapping), copies the
NUL-terminated bytes at `p` into a new string of the program's own.** It is the
copy a `string` result makes, offered for the pointers a `string` result cannot
be: the ones C allocated for the caller to free. The program copies, then frees
C's buffer itself (`tests/cases/ffi_owned_string`,
[cookbook](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/IR_COOKBOOK.md#readcstring-a-string-out-of-a-buffer-c-owns)):

```ts
import { readCString } from "nish:unsafe";

declare function strdup(s: string): CPtr | null;
declare function free(p: CPtr): void;

function owned(s: string): string {
  const p = strdup(s);
  if (p === null) {
    return "";
  }
  const copy = readCString(p);
  free(p);
  return copy;
}
```

```llvm
if.end:
  %6 = load i8*, i8** %p.addr, align 8
  %7 = call i8* @nish.ffi.str(i8* %6)
  store i8* %7, i8** %copy.addr, align 8
  %8 = load i8*, i8** %p.addr, align 8
  call void @free(i8* %8)
```

- **It is `nish:unsafe` because nothing proves the bytes end.** The copy scans
  for the NUL with the `@nish.ffi.str` helper a `string` result uses, and a
  pointer that is dangling, already freed, or to a buffer with no NUL is
  undefined behaviour: the import is the author's word, as `uncheckedGet`'s is.
  So the call is an `unchecked` [panic site](semantics-decisions.md#panic-sites) that is allowed
  under `--deny-panics`, beside the copy's `oom`; it is an `unsafe` call to
  `--deny unsafe`, and the `CPtr` it reads came from a `declare function`,
  which is `ffi`.
- **`NULL` cannot reach it from a `CPtr | null`.** The parameter is `CPtr`, so
  an unnarrowed pointer is
  `` `readCString` expects an argument of type CPtr, got CPtr | null ``
  (`reject_unsafe_read_cstring`) and `if (p !== null)` comes first. What the
  compiler trusts is the declaration: a `declare function` whose result is
  declared `CPtr` gets no check after the call, so a C function that may
  answer `NULL` and is declared `CPtr` hands `readCString` a `NULL` it reads
  through. Declare such a result `CPtr | null`.
- **The copy is new on every call and is the calling function's allocation**,
  as a `string` result's is: kept past a loop's pass, returned, stored by a
  constructor and released with its owner, and refused inside a `using a =
  arena()` block that would release one held outside it (`` `readCString(p)` may
  be allocated inside the `using arena()` block ``,
  `reject_ffi_owned_string_arena`). C's buffer is never held past the call, so
  `free(p)` straight after it is safe.
- **On wasm32 it lowers to the same helper.** `@nish.ffi.str` is a byte scan and
  a `nish_str_new`, which every runtime has, so `readCString` adds nothing to
  the link; whether the program links there is the `declare function`'s
  question, answered by the libc the target has.

### A `u8[]` parameter: a buffer and its count

**A `u8[]` or `readonly u8[]` parameter is a buffer C reads or writes, and a
run of one or more of them is followed by exactly one `u64`: the byte count C
may touch in every buffer of the run.** Pairing the count by position is the
declaration's word, not a proof. `fwrite(ptr, size, nmemb, stream)` touches
`size * nmemb` bytes, so declared as `fwrite(buf: readonly u8[], size: u64,
nmemb: u64, f: CPtr)` it pairs `size` with the buffer, and `fwrite(buf, 1,
1000, f)` on a 10-byte array overflows it. The safe spelling declares the size
as the count and passes `1` as `nmemb`: `fwrite(buf: readonly u8[], n: u64,
one: u64, f: CPtr)`, called as `fwrite(buf, n, 1, f)`. Nothing stops a call from
passing another `nmemb`, which is the same class of mistake as declaring `free`
with two parameters.

```ts
declare function memcpy(dst: u8[], src: readonly u8[], n: u64): CPtr;
declare function getentropy(buf: u8[], n: u64): i32;
declare function compare(a: readonly u8[], na: u64, b: readonly u8[], nb: u64): i32;
```

- **`memcpy(dst, src, n)` is one run of two buffers sharing a count**, and
  `(a, na, b, nb)` is two runs with a count each (`tests/cases/ffi_buffer_declared`).
  The same array passed twice in one run, `memcpy(a, a, n)`, is not refused:
  C sees two pointers to one block, and overlapping `memcpy` is undefined in C
  (`memmove` is the one that allows it).
- **`readonly u8[]` is C's `const`.** A `u8[]` parameter says C may write the
  bytes; a `readonly u8[]` says it only reads them. C can cast the `const`
  away, and the compiler cannot check that.
- **A run with no count after it is refused**, with `` takes the buffer `md`
  with no count after it: a run of `u8[]` parameters is followed by one `u64` ``
  (`reject_ffi_buffer_length_missing`, `SHA256(d, n, md)`'s fixed-size output),
  and so is a count of any other type, `` and the parameter after a run of
  `u8[]` buffers is their byte count, a `u64` `` (`reject_ffi_buffer_length_type`).
- **Only `u8` crosses.** `i32[]` or `f64[]` is
  `` the only array a declared C function takes is a `u8[]` or a `readonly u8[]` ``
  (`reject_ffi_buffer_element`).
- **A buffer is never null and never a result.** `u8[] | null` is refused
  (`reject_ffi_buffer_nullable`, and `reject_ffi_buffer_nullable_in_run` for one
  inside a run): it has no length to hold the count to, so the
  `NULL, 0` call C allows is declared with a `CPtr | null` parameter. A `u8[]`
  result is refused by the return rule above (`reject_ffi_buffer_return`).
- **A call passes the array's data block, and checks the count against every
  buffer of its run first.** Each buffer is lowered to its data pointer, a
  `uint8_t *` (`i8*` in the IR), and the count is compared, unsigned, with the
  buffer's length before C runs. A count larger than one of them stops the
  program with an `ffi-length` panic, `` `write`: argument 3 (n) counts more
  bytes than argument 2 (buf) holds ``, exit 1 (`tests/cases/panics_ffi_length`,
  and `panics_ffi_length_memcpy` for the shorter buffer of a run). The count is
  a `u64`, so `toU64(0) - toU64(1)` is the largest count there is, and fails
  (`panics_ffi_length_wrapped`).
- **The pointer and the length are read after the last argument is
  evaluated**, so C sees the array as it is at the call: an argument that
  pushes or pops before it is seen (`tests/cases/ffi_buffer_late_load`,
  `panics_ffi_length_shrink`, `panics_ffi_length_inline_pop`).
- **One count is proved: `toU64(b.length)` of the buffer itself**, where `b`
  is a `const` local or a parameter named alone and no later argument may
  resize an array. Such a call carries no check and is not a panic site, so
  `read(fd, buf, toU64(buf.length))` compiles under `--deny-panics`. A field
  path, an alias of the buffer, another array's length and a literal are
  checked (`tests/cases/ffi_buffer_count_proved`). `--deny-panics` refuses
  any other count and names the one it accepts: `` pass `toU64(buf.length)`
  of the buffer itself, which needs no check ``.
- **C borrows the bytes for the call, and writes through a `u8[]`.** As with
  a `string`, the pointer is lent for the length of the call and C may not
  keep it, so a buffer made in the call's arena scope is released after it
  (`tests/cases/ffi_buffer_read`). A `u8[]` argument is written by the call
  and a `readonly u8[]` one is not, and the compiler records it as it records
  a store. An exported function that hands its own `u8[]` parameter to such a
  call writes that parameter: its header drops the `const`, the wasm glue
  copies the bytes back, and its `define` loses `readonly`
  (`tests/cases/ffi_buffer_export_written`). A task a scope spawns may not
  reach such a call: C's body is unseen, so the call may write memory the
  parent can see, and the task is refused with `` writes memory its caller
  can see `` (`reject_ffi_buffer_call_spawn`, and
  `reject_ffi_buffer_scope_race`, `reject_ffi_buffer_scope_field_race` and
  `reject_ffi_buffer_scope_element_race` for a call reached through a
  function).
- **Every kind of call site lowers the same way**: a call by name, through a
  function parameter bound to the declaration, in a constructor reached by
  `new` and in a method (`tests/cases/ffi_buffer_call_sites`), and a call that
  passes a buffer is refused by `--deny ffi` like any other foreign call.
- **On wasm32 a `u64` count is wider than C's `size_t`.** The data pointer is
  32 bits there and the length check is the same 64-bit compare, but a C
  function whose count is a `size_t` takes 32 bits: declare its count `u64`
  only on a target where `size_t` is 64 bits, until a later release gives the
  count a target-width type. A freestanding wasm build (`--target wasm32`)
  refuses a `declare function`, so a buffer declaration is for `--profile
  wasi` there (see "Host modules" below).

### A handle class: a class that owns a `CPtr`

**A class with a `CPtr` or `CPtr | null` field is a handle class: it owns the C
resource the pointer names, and its `[Symbol.dispose]` names the C function
that closes it** (`tests/cases/ffi_handle_positions`, `docs/wp53-ffi-buffers-handles.md`
§4a–§4d).

```ts
declare function fopen(path: string, mode: string): CPtr | null;
declare function fclose(p: CPtr): i32;
declare function fgetc(p: CPtr): i32;

class File {
  readonly file: CPtr | null;
  constructor(path: string) {
    this.file = fopen(path, "r");
  }
  read(): i32 {
    const p = this.file;
    if (p === null) {
      return -1;
    }
    return fgetc(p);
  }
  [Symbol.dispose](): void {
    const p = this.file;
    if (p !== null) {
      fclose(p);
    }
  }
}

const first = (f: File): i32 => f.read();
```

**`using` of a handle class closes it at every exit of its block, once.**
`using f = new File(p)` opens `f` as soon as its initialiser returns, before a
later declarator's initialiser runs, and calls the close its
`[Symbol.dispose]` names on every way control leaves the block: falling off
its end, `return`, `break`, `continue`, and an `orReturn()` that propagates,
including one in a later declarator's initialiser. A `return` computes its
value first and closes after it, so `return twice(n)` inside the block is not
a tail call. Each declarator opens before the next one's initialiser runs.
Falling off the end, `break` and `continue` close the declarators in the
reverse of the order they opened, beside an arena, a scope or a lock in the
same `using`. A `return` or a propagating `orReturn()` joins every `scope()`
before its value is computed (the value may read what the tasks stored), then
closes the handles and gives back the locks, innermost first, then releases
the arenas (`ffi_handle_file`, `ffi_handle_exits`, `ffi_handle_arena`,
`ffi_handle_shapes`, `tests/link/ffi_handle_mutex`,
`tests/link/using_declarator_exit`). The close is inlined as the dispose spells
it: the field is loaded and the C function called with it, behind a `null`
test only when the dispose writes one (`const p = this.f; if (p !== null)`);
a dispose that is the single call `close(this.f)` calls it with the field as
it is, `null` included (`ffi_handle_shapes`). The `using` is where the program reaches `ffi`, so
`--deny ffi` refuses it and names the close (`caps_ffi_handle`,
`reject_ffi_handle_deny`).

A panic and `process.exit` do not close: the process ends, and the operating
system takes back the descriptor. What it does not take back is what a C
library still buffers. `panic`, `expect` and a failed range entry end through
`exit(1)`, which flushes stdio, but a failed check and out of memory end
through `_exit(1)`, which does not, so bytes written to a `FILE *` with
`fwrite` and not yet flushed are lost on a bounds panic. Flush (`fflush`)
before code that may panic when those bytes matter.

- **The class.** Exactly one `CPtr` or `CPtr | null` field, `readonly` and with
  no initialiser (`reject_ffi_handle_two_fields`, `_field_mutable`,
  `_field_initialiser`). No type parameters, no `implements`, no `export`
  (`_generic_class`, `_implements`, `_export`), and no `static readonly json`
  (`_json`).
- **The write.** The constructor writes the field once, as
  `this.file = g(...)` at its top level, with `g` a `declare function` and no
  exit before it (`_field_copy`, `_field_copy_twice`, `_field_copy_branch`,
  `_field_copy_non_foreign`).
- **The read.** The pointer is read only as `this.file` inside a method of the
  class, passed straight to a `declare function` or bound once to a `const`
  (`_field_read_outside`, `_field_other_instance`, `_field_alias_copy`,
  `_field_alias_let`, `_field_position`): `` The pointer `file` of handle class
  `File` cannot be used here ``.
- **The close.** `[Symbol.dispose](): void` is `close(this.file);` or
  `const p = this.file; if (p !== null) { close(p); }` for a `declare
  function` `close` of one parameter (`_no_dispose`, `_dispose_body`,
  `_dispose_arity`, `_dispose_arg_type`, `_dispose_unknown`, `_dispose_forms`,
  `_dispose_shapes`). A class declares one, with no modifier
  (`_dispose_twice`, `_dispose_static`). Nothing else may
  call that close on the field, in a method or in the constructor
  (`_close_call`), and `[Symbol.dispose]` is never called by name
  (`_dispose_call`).
- **Where a `File` may be.** It is opened by `using` (once lowered), called
  (`f.read()`), or lent to a parameter of type `File`, which may lend it on.
  Everything else is `` A `File` cannot be used here `` (`_position`): `new`
  outside a `using` initialiser, `this` leaving the constructor, a copy into
  another binding, an array element, an object literal, a capture, a builtin's
  argument, a comparison (`_new_outside_using`, `_this_escapes`, `_alias`,
  `_array`, `_object_literal`, `_closure_capture`, `_builtin_arg`,
  `_walk_compare`).
- **Where `File` may be written.** Only as the type of such a parameter. A
  local's annotation, a field, a return, a `Result` arm, a nullable, a type
  argument and an exported function's parameter are `` `File` is a handle
  class, and its name may be written only as the type of a parameter that
  borrows one `` (`_type_position`, `_field`, `_return`, `_result`,
  `_nullable`, `_type_argument`, `_exported_param`).
- **Not after its close, and not kept past a lend.** A `using` binding's scope
  is its block, which ends where the close is emitted, so a handle named after
  its block — after it, in the loop's next iteration, in a `do` loop's
  condition, in a `for` loop's update, in a later `case`, in the `else`, later
  in a constructor — names nothing: `` Unknown builtin `f.read` `` or
  `` Unknown identifier `f` `` (`_use_after_close`, `_use_after_close_loop`,
  `_use_after_close_do_while`, `_use_after_close_for_update`,
  `_use_after_close_switch`, `_use_after_close_else`, `_use_after_close_ctor`).
  A `using` written straight into a `case` clause is refused by the clause rule
  (`_use_after_close_switch_clause`). A lent handle cannot be kept by its
  callee. The value rule refuses a local (`let saved = f`,
  `_use_after_close_keep`), an alias (`_alias`), an array (`_array`) and a
  `scope()` task (`_scope_task`); the type rule refuses a return (`_return`)
  and a type argument (`_type_argument`), among them a `Map` or a `Channel` of
  the class (`_use_after_close_keep_map`, `_use_after_close_keep_channel`);
  both refuse a field of another class, set in a method, through `new` or as
  `h.l = this` (`_use_after_close_keep_field`, `_walk_ctor_param`,
  `_use_after_close_keep_this`). Some shapes are refused by a general
  rule first: a closure by the arrow-capture rule (`_closure_capture`), and a
  module binding by the absence of a top-level `let` and the rule that a
  module constant is never assigned (`_use_after_close_keep_module`,
  `_use_after_close_keep_module_expr`). In its own constructor `this` is half
  built, and is neither lent, called, stored nor aliased (`_ctor_this_lend`,
  `_ctor_this_receiver`, `_ctor_this_store`, `_ctor_this_alias`).

**Two things stay C contracts, as a buffer's count does.** The class's methods
pass the field only to functions that use it and return, and that neither close
what it owns nor hand it back: `freopen`, a close through a C wrapper with
another name, `close(fileno(p))`, or a C function returning its argument are
not seen by the rules above. And the constructor's foreign call returns a
pointer the object owns: two objects built from one shared pointer would both
close it.

### A `declare class`: a C struct, lent by pointer

**A `declare class` is a C struct: its fields are laid out in declaration order,
each at its natural alignment, and the size is rounded up to the widest
alignment, as a C compiler lays out the same fields. `new Name()` takes no
arguments and zero-fills it, and a `declare function` parameter typed `Name`
borrows it as a `struct Name *`** (`tests/cases/ffi_struct_param`,
`ffi_struct_layout`, [cookbook](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/IR_COOKBOOK.md#declare-class-a-c-struct-lent-by-pointer),
`docs/wp27-ffi.md` §9b):

```ts
declare class Timespec {
  sec: i64
  nsec: i64
}
declare function clock_gettime(clock: i32, ts: Timespec): i32

const now = new Timespec()
clock_gettime(1, now)
console.log(now.sec)
```

```llvm
%struct.Timespec = type { i64, i64 }
declare i32 @clock_gettime(i32, %struct.Timespec*)
  %Timespec.obj = alloca %struct.Timespec, align 8
  %0 = bitcast %struct.Timespec* %Timespec.obj to i8*
  call void @llvm.memset.p0i8.i64(i8* align 8 %0, i8 0, i64 16, i1 false)
  store %struct.Timespec* %Timespec.obj, %struct.Timespec** %now.addr, align 8
  %1 = load %struct.Timespec*, %struct.Timespec** %now.addr, align 8
  %2 = call i32 @clock_gettime(i32 1, %struct.Timespec* %1)
```

- **`new` zero-fills every byte, padding included**, with one `llvm.memset` of
  the struct's size: C may compare or hash the whole struct, and a
  `zeroinitializer` store need not write the padding (`ffi_struct_layout`).
- **A `CPtr` field is the target's `void *`**: eight bytes natively, four under
  `--profile wasi` (wasm32), where the struct's size and offsets are the ones
  clang gives the same C struct for that target (`tests/ffi-struct.js`).
- **A field is `i32`, `i64`, `u8`, `u16`, `u32`, `u64`, `f32`, `f64`, `CPtr`,
  `CPtr | null`, or another `declare class`, embedded by value** — C's
  `struct timespec it_value;`, not a pointer to one. A `number` field is
  refused whatever the mode, since `--number-mode` picks its width and a C
  struct has one layout: `` has type `number`, whose width `--number-mode`
  chooses `` (NL2755, `reject_ffi_struct_field_number`). Any other type is
  `` Field `ok` of `declare class Flags` has type `boolean`, which has no C
  layout `` (NL2752, `reject_ffi_struct_field_type`, `reject_cls_declare`,
  `reject_ffi_struct_field_array`, `reject_ffi_struct_field_class`): a
  `boolean`, a `string`, an array and a Nish class have no C spelling the
  compiler could promise. A struct cannot embed
  itself, directly or through another (NL2749, `reject_ffi_struct_self`,
  `reject_ffi_struct_cycle`).
- **A field is plain and has no initializer, and the class has nothing but
  fields**: no `readonly`, `static` or optional field (NL2747), no initializer,
  because `new` zero-fills (NL2748), no constructor, method, accessor or other
  member such as an index signature (NL2751, `reject_ffi_struct_index_signature`), no type parameter (NL2741), no `extends` or `implements` (NL2750),
  and no `export` (NL2746) — each pinned by a `reject_ffi_struct_*` case.
- **It stays in its module.** It cannot be a parameter or the return type of an
  exported function or an exported class's method, or a field of an exported
  class or interface: `` `declare class Point` cannot be a parameter of an
  exported function `` (`reject_ffi_struct_export_param`, `_return`, `_method`,
  `_field`). A type that holds one is refused there too, however deep —
  through `Result`, `T | null`, an array, a generic instance or a class of
  this program: `` `Wrap` holds a `declare class Point` and cannot be a
  parameter of an exported function `` (NL2756,
  `reject_ffi_struct_export_result`, `_generic`, `_holder`). So no `.d.ts`
  or N-API binding ever describes one, and `--emit-header`, which lists every
  class of the program, declares a class that holds one only as an opaque
  `typedef struct Holder Holder;` (`tests/ffi-struct.js`, `docs/wp27-ffi.md`
  §9g).
- **It is a native build's.** A wasm module a page loads — freestanding wasm,
  or any build that writes `--emit-dts` — links no C to lend a struct to, and
  its IR is laid out for wasm32 later: `` `declare class Point` declares a C
  struct, and a wasm module a page loads links no C to lend it to `` (NL2757).
  A `--profile wasi` build is wasm32 from the start and keeps it.
- **It is built with `new` and nothing else.** `new Point(1)` is refused as for
  any class without a constructor (`reject_ffi_struct_new_args`), and an object
  literal typed as one is
  `` an object literal cannot lay out a C struct `` (NL2744,
  `reject_ffi_struct_literal`).
- **C borrows it for the length of the call**, as it borrows a `string`: it may
  read and write the fields until it returns, and may not keep the address. The
  escape analysis treats the argument as a read, so an instance that does not
  otherwise escape stays in the caller's stack frame; a C function that keeps
  the pointer (an `aio_read` control block, a struct handed to a thread) is
  outside the contract. Its accesses carry no TBAA tag, so a field read after
  the call sees what C wrote, and a function of this program that passes its
  parameter on to C writes through that parameter, so the parameter is not
  `readonly` and its caller's read sees the write too (`ffi_struct_param`).
- **`Name | null` passes `NULL` for `null`**, under the rule a `CPtr | null`
  parameter follows: the literal `null`, or a value narrowed with `!== null`
  (NL2539, `reject_ffi_struct_nullable_held`).
- **An embedded struct is part of its owner.** `stamp.at.sec` reads and writes a
  field in place, and `clock_gettime(1, stamp.at)` lends C the address inside
  `stamp`; those are the only two uses. Holding it — `const at = stamp.at`, or
  passing it to a function this program defines — is
  `` cannot be held as a value `` (NL2743, `reject_ffi_struct_nested_bind`,
  `reject_ffi_struct_nested_nish_arg`), and replacing it is
  `` a `declare class` embedded in its object is written field by field ``
  (NL2745, `reject_ffi_struct_nested_assign`).
- **It is not a return type or an array element.** C returning a struct by
  value, or a pointer into memory it owns, leaves the copy with no owner on
  this side: `` a C struct is only lent to C by pointer: take a `Point`
  parameter for C to fill `` (NL2742, `reject_ffi_struct_return`); an array of
  them would be a C array the program lays out element by element, and is
  `` cannot be an array element `` (NL2740, `reject_ffi_struct_array`,
  `reject_ffi_struct_array_literal`, `reject_ffi_struct_array_new`), however
  the array's type is spelled.
- **Its fields are C's to fill.** Typed JSON does not decode into one or
  encode one: `` a `declare class`: C reads and writes its fields `` (NL2753,
  `reject_ffi_struct_json`). A spread copies a flat one's fields into a class
  of this program, but not one that embeds another, whose embedded struct is
  not a value: `` which a spread cannot copy `` (NL2754,
  `reject_ffi_struct_spread`).
- **`--emit-ts` refuses a module that declares one**, with the same message as
  for a `declare function` (NL4010): it is C's layout, and JavaScript has none.

### What a declaration cannot say

Each of these is refused, and each refusal is pinned by a case:

- **A variadic C function, spelled variadically.** A rest parameter is
  `Rest parameters are not supported here` before its type is read, `...bytes:
  u8[]` included (`reject_ffi_variadic`, `reject_ffi_buffer_rest`). A variadic function declared with a
  fixed arity, `printf(fmt: string, x: i32)`, is accepted and is the
  declaration's contract: the compiler cannot tell `open` is variadic from its
  name.
- **`syscall`, by name**: `` `declare function syscall` is refused ``
  (`reject_ffi_syscall`). It is variadic and bypasses libc; declare the libc
  function that wraps the system call.
- **A callback.** C never calls into Nish: an arrow passed to a declared C
  function is refused (`reject_ffi_callback`), and a
  [function reference](#function-references) is a tag only this program's
  dispatchers read, not an address, so it is not a `CPtr` either.
- **A read through a `CPtr`.** `p[0]` is `Cannot index a value of type CPtr`
  (`reject_ffi_pointer_deref`); `readCString` above is the one read.
- **Inline assembly.** `asm("nop")` is an unknown function (`reject_ffi_asm`).
- **An allocator from C memory.** `arena()` takes no argument, so `using a =
  arena(p)` is refused (`reject_ffi_allocator`).

**A foreign declaration has no body** (`reject_ffi_body`) and **cannot be
`export`ed** (`reject_ffi_export`), because `export` offers other modules a
function *this* module defines.

**A declared function's symbol is its name as written, in whatever package
declares it.** A function a package defines carries the package's prefix
(`@probe.probeAbs`), but a `declare function` names the C function, and C has
one namespace, so a package or a `std/` module that declares `abs` calls `@abs`
exactly as the program's own modules do (`tests/link/ffi_package_declare`).
**Two declarations of one name must agree**: the same parameter and return
types, which is what a C prototype is, so parameter names and the aliases a
type is spelled through do not count (`tests/link/ffi_package_declare_same`).
Agreeing declarations are one C function, whether they are in two packages or
in two modules of the same package, which was refused as a duplicate symbol
before. Declarations that disagree are refused, naming both:
`` C has one namespace, so every `declare function` of one name must agree on
its parameter and return types ``. A buffer's `readonly`, a `| null` and the
number of parameters each count (`tests/link/ffi_package_declare_clash`,
`tests/link/ffi_package_declare_mismatch`). So is a function whose emitted
symbol is a declared name: an exported function of the program's own package,
or a private one whose name is not reserved to C:
`` a `declare function` binds the C symbol of its name in every package, so
rename the defined function `` (`tests/link/ffi_package_declare_root_clash`).
A private function named like a C library function is emitted as `abs$`, and a
generic one's instantiations as `labs$i32`, so neither takes the C symbol and
both are accepted (`tests/link/ffi_package_declare_apart`). The two refusals
are refused rather than linked because the whole-program analysis keeps one
set of facts per symbol, and the two would share it.

**The declaration carries no LLVM attributes, and its callers pay for it.**
Nothing about a body the compiler cannot see is provable, so a function that
calls C loses `readnone` and `willreturn`, and so does everything above it in the
call graph; a function that calls no C keeps both (`tests/cases/ffi_scalar`).
`nounwind` is the one exception, and it is a **decision rather than a proof**:
unwinding out of a foreign call is undefined in this language, the same position
clang takes compiling C, because there is no `throw` and no landing pad with
which to do anything else. See
[`docs/wp27-ffi.md`](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp27-ffi.md) §2 and the
[cookbook entry](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/IR_COOKBOOK.md#declare-function-calling-c).

**A program that calls C is no longer one the compiler can reason about end to
end.** That is the trade the feature is: the whole-program fact fixpoint is the
performance thesis, and a foreign call is a hole in it.

**And it is outside the differential oracle by construction.** The oracle
runs a program's frozen JavaScript rewrite against `runtime/shim.mjs`, on the
premise that the same source means the same thing in both worlds; that premise
does not hold for a source whose meaning is "whatever this C function does"
([wp27-ffi.md](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/wp27-ffi.md) §5). The evidence for an FFI program is arranged the
other way round: a golden `.ll`, an `llvm-as` pass, a native round trip against
real libc, and the attribute assertions.

### Host modules: the functions a page supplies

**A wasm module calls a function of the page that loads it by importing it
from a host module**: a TypeScript file of the page's, named by `--host
<file>` or by the root `package.json`'s `"nish": { "host": [...] }`
(`tests/host-import`, `docs/wp50-wasm-host.md` §3). An import from any other
file is an ordinary Nish import.

```ts
// host.ts, the page's
import type { f64, u32 } from "nish";
export type Canvas = HostHandle<"canvas">;
export function fill(c: Canvas, rgb: u32): void { canvases[c].fill(rgb); }
export function nowMs(): f64 { return performance.now(); }
```

```llvm
declare void @fill(i32, i32) #1
attributes #1 = { "wasm-import-module"="host" "wasm-import-name"="fill" }
```

- **Only the exported signatures are read.** Each `export function`'s
  parameter and result types, each exported `enum`, and each
  `export type X = HostHandle<"kind">`. A function body is skipped as a
  balanced run of tokens, so it may use anything TypeScript has. Text the
  lexer cannot skip, a regex literal or JSX, refuses the file with
  `` move that code into a module the host file imports `` (NL3049); other
  statements are skipped unread.
- **What crosses.** The integer and float widths, `boolean`, a ranged integer,
  an enum, a `HostHandle`, a `string` parameter, and `void` as a result. `i64`
  and `u64` are a `bigint` on the page's side
  (`import type { i64 } from "nish"`). Refused, each naming the explicit form:
  an object, a class, a function, `unknown` or `any` (NL2661), a generic
  function (NL2662), a `Promise` (NL2663) and a `string` result (NL2667): the
  page writes text into module storage instead (`nish/host/text`). An array
  crosses only as a buffer window, below.
- **A `string` argument is its UTF-8 bytes, lent for the call.** It lowers to
  two wasm values, the address of the string's bytes and their count, read
  from the string's own header, so nothing is copied on the module's side;
  the loader's wrapper decodes them with `TextDecoder` into a JS string before
  the page's function runs, and an invalid sequence becomes U+FFFD. The
  string may be a literal, a concatenation or a template; one the module
  built lives in the export's arena, which is released after the export
  returns (`tests/cases/host_import_string`; `tests/run.js`, section
  `host-import-text`;
  [cookbook](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/IR_COOKBOOK.md#a-string-to-the-page-its-bytes-and-their-count)):

  ```ts
  // web/host.ts
  export function say(s: string): void { console.log(s); }
  // app.ts
  say(`hello ${n}`);
  ```

  ```llvm
  declare void @say(i8*, i32) #2
  %1 = call i8* @nish_str_concat(i8* bitcast ({ i64, [7 x i8] }* @.str.0 to i8*), i8* %0)
  %2 = bitcast i8* %1 to i64*
  %3 = load i64, i64* %2, align 8
  %4 = trunc i64 %3 to i32
  %5 = getelementptr inbounds i8, i8* %1, i64 8
  call void @say(i8* %5, i32 %4)
  ```
- **Each host function is a declaration with the wasm import attributes**:
  module `host`, its own name. It carries no other attribute, and its callers
  lose `readnone` and `willreturn` as for a C declaration. `wasm-ld` makes it
  an import with no `--allow-undefined`.
- **A host module exists only in a freestanding wasm build.** A native or
  `--target wasm32-wasi` build that imports one is refused (NL3050). A build
  that makes a page module (`--target wasm32`, or `--emit-dts` with no
  `--target`) refuses a `declare function` (NL2666): the module links no C, so
  the declaration would be an import the page does not supply. `--target
  wasm32-wasi --emit-dts` links C, so it keeps `declare function` legal.
- **The loader and its types.** `--emit-dts` adds
  `Imports = { host: typeof import("./host") }` to the `.d.ts`, and `load`
  takes it. The loader passes a function through by reference when every
  value crosses as it stands, and wraps it once, at `load`, when a value
  converts. A `u32` or `u64` argument arrives signed and is read unsigned
  (`>>> 0`, `BigInt.asUintN(64, …)`); a `u8` or `u16` argument needs nothing,
  since the module zero-extends it. A `u8` or `u16` result is masked, a
  `boolean` crosses as 0 or 1, and a ranged integer result is checked by the
  loader's `rangeOut` (`RangeError` naming the function).
- **`--emit-ts` keeps the import** as written, pointing at the host file, so
  the TypeScript reading calls the same functions.
- **A call to a host function is an `ffi` call**: `--deny ffi` refuses it and
  `--emit-capabilities` names it.

**An array crosses as a buffer window: the array, then `at: u32, n: u32`**
(`tests/host-window`, `docs/wp50-wasm-host.md` §5.3). The host lends the page
the elements `[at, at + n)` of the array the program passes, in place, with no
copy:

```ts
// host.ts, the page's
import type { u32 } from "nish";

export function doubleF32(xs: Float32Array, at: u32, n: u32): void {
  for (let i = at; i < at + n; i++) xs[i] *= 2;
}
```

```ts
// the program
const DATA = new Float32Array(64)
export const tick = (): void => { doubleF32(DATA, 16, 8) }
```

- **Six elements lend**: `u8[]`, `u16[]`, `u32[]`, `i32[]`, `f32[]` and
  `f64[]`, their `readonly` forms and their typed-array names. Any other
  array is NL2681 (`` a buffer window lends only `u8[]`, `u16[]`, `u32[]`,
  `i32[]`, `f32[]` or `f64[]` (or the typed array of each): copy the values
  into one of those ``). The two parameters after it must be there (NL2682,
  `` a buffer window with no `at: u32, n: u32` after it ``) and be `u32`, the
  width of a wasm32 address (NL2683). NL2664, which refused every typed array
  before windows existed, is retired.
- **The window is checked in the module, before the page runs.** `at` and `n`
  are zero-extended and added in `i64`, so a sum that wraps in 32 bits still
  fails, and held against the array's length; past the end is an `ffi-length`
  panic,
  `` `doubleF32`: argument 2 (at) plus argument 3 (n) reaches past the end of argument 1 (xs) ``,
  numbered and named from the host function's own parameters
  ([cookbook](https://github.com/amritk/nish/blob/main/docs/IR_COOKBOOK.md#a-host-buffer-window-checked-in-i64)). A call
  that lends `0, toU32(xs.length)` of a local array `xs` is proven in bounds
  and emits no check. A window of module storage always keeps the check,
  even `0, toU32(DATA.length)`: the range pass proves facts about locals,
  not about storage.
- **What the page gets is a view of all of memory and an index.** The
  loader's adapter passes a whole-memory view of the element type, the
  array's first element plus `at` as the index, and `n`, so the host
  function's `xs[at]` is the program's `DATA[at]`. A page that indexes outside
  `[at, at + n)` reaches the rest of the module: the page is trusted, and it
  reads only its window ([security record](../../security/wasm-host.md)).
- **Module storage lends to a window** like any array of a lending element,
  and so does a local array. A record storage does not.

**Module storage is the page's view of the module.** Under
`--profile wasm-host` the link exports each storage's data, and `--emit-dts`
types what the loader builds from it:

- **`layout`**, a `Layout` with one entry per storage, keyed by its name (by
  its symbol when two modules export the same name):
  `{ at, length, stride, fields? }`, where `at` is the byte address in
  `memory`, `stride` the element's size, and `fields` each record field's
  byte offset within the element. `length`, `stride` and each offset are
  literal types in the `.d.ts`, so a page that hard-codes one, or reads a
  field the module does not have, fails `tsc` once the layout changes. `at`
  is read from the instance at load and never moves. A record field is read
  through the whole-memory view of its width:
  `views().f32[(layout.bodies.at + i * layout.bodies.stride + layout.bodies.fields.x) >> 2]`.
- **`views()`**, the whole memory as `buffer` and as each typed array (`u8`,
  `i8`, `u16`, `i16`, `u32`, `i32`, `f32`, `f64`, `i64`, `u64`), and
  `storage.<key>`, a typed view of each scalar storage (a `boolean` one as
  `Uint8Array`, an enum or range as `Int32Array`, a `HostHandle` as
  `Uint32Array`). `views()` answers the same object until a growing memory
  replaces `memory.buffer`, so a page calls it again after any call into the
  module rather than keeping one view across calls.

**Under `--profile wasm-host` a panic is the page's to report**, in a
program with [module storage](#module-storage) or a
[host module](#host-modules-the-functions-a-page-supplies)
(`tests/panic`, `docs/wp50-wasm-host.md` §6). The `nish.panic` import,
`NishPanic`, the dead module, `NishReentry` (below), and the `onPanic` and
`sites` options of `load` and `loadSync` are for such a program only;
`loadSync` itself is in every loader.
Any other program gets the `.wasm`, loader and `.d.ts` it got before: a panic
is a bare `RuntimeError` trap, the module stays usable, and its next call
runs. The module of such a program imports one function
from module `nish`, `panic`, and every runtime panic calls it with its kind
and the words it would print natively; the loader turns that into an
exception:

- **The call that panicked throws `NishPanic`**, an `Error` whose `message` is
  the native text (`index out of range: 9 >= 4`,
  `slice out of range: [a, b) of length len`, an overflow's text,
  `out of memory`, `the program exited with code 3`, or `panic(…)`'s own
  words) and which carries `kind` (`panic`, `index`, `slice`, `overflow`,
  `memory`, `exit`, `divide`, or `trap`, `reentry` or `exception` for a
  module that died some other way) and `site`, the panic site's number
  (-1 for none). An array's `xs.slice` out of range throws with `kind`
  `panic`, not `slice`: its check is `std/array.ts`'s own `panic(...)`,
  though the message reads as string `slice`'s does.
- **Before it throws, the loader calls `onPanic`.** `load(bytes, { onPanic,
  sites })` takes the reporter; the default, `reportPanic` from `nish/page`,
  writes `nish: <message>` to `console.error`, as a native program writes it
  to stderr. An exception the reporter throws is swallowed: the `NishPanic` is
  thrown either way.
- **`sites` names where.** The wasm-host link writes `<out>.sites.json`
  (`app.wasm.sites.json` for `-o app.wasm`),
  `[{ kind, at }]` with one entry per panic site, indexed by `site`. Passed to
  `load` (parsed), it ends each message with ` at path:line:col`; without it
  the message is the native text alone. Under `--profile wasm` the module
  imports nothing and each panic is a bare trap, with no message and no
  site; the same loader still marks the module dead on it, so later calls
  throw as above.
- **A panic ends the module.** Its memory survives, as it was, for a page
  that reads it, but every later call throws `NishPanic`
  (`the module is dead: …`) before the module runs. An exception a host
  import throws out of a call ends the module the same way, since the call it
  interrupted never finished.
- **A bad argument does not end it.** The loader checks every argument's
  shape before the module runs: a number of the wrong type or range, a
  `Result` that is not an object with a boolean `ok` and a payload of its arm's
  type, an array argument whose brand (read off `%TypedArray%.prototype`, not
  `instanceof`) is not the typed array it names. Each throws a `TypeError`; an
  error a `Result` argument's getter throws reaches the caller as it is. Either
  way the module never ran and stays alive (`tests/run.js`, section `panic`:
  `badarg`, `badshape`).

**One call at a time.** A host import that calls an export while a call into
the module is still running gets `NishReentry` (`a call into the module was
made while another call into it was running`), and the inner call never runs.
The reporter is different: the module is already dead when `onPanic` runs, so
an export it calls throws `NishPanic` (`the module is dead: …`). The outer call's state is half changed at that point, which
is why the loader refuses rather than runs it (`docs/security/wasm-host.md`,
WH-3). Left uncaught, the `NishReentry` escapes the outer call too, and like
any exception out of a call it ends the module. A page that needs the
module's answer schedules the call for after the import returns. In a module
that links the runtime, a call also gives back, once its result is read,
everything it allocated in the arena, so a long-lived page does not grow the
module's memory call by call.

**`HostHandle<K>` is a nominal `i32` for an object the page keeps**
(`docs/wp50-wasm-host.md` §4). `K` is a string literal type, and
`HostHandle<"a">` and `HostHandle<"b">` are different types, here and under
`tsc`, where `runtime/nish.d.ts` makes it a branded `number` or `0`, so `tsc`
also refuses any number but `0` where a handle is wanted. A handle supports `===` and
`!==` against a handle of its kind or `0` ("none"), and is stored wherever a
scalar is; it has no arithmetic and no conversion to or from a number, so it
is made only by a host function that returns one. A field's or a parameter's
default may only be `0` (NL2670). A second type argument, or
a kind that is not a string literal of letters, digits and `_`, is NL2669, and a string literal type
anywhere but a `HostHandle`'s kind is NL2668. It lowers to
`i32`, so a program with no host module emits nothing new.
